## 10. Saṅghabhedasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

10. In the commentary on the Saṅghabheda training rule, 'a concordant Saṅgha' (samagga saṅgha) refers to the community of bhikkhus who are united, being inseparable both in mind and in body. For this very reason, it is stated in the word-for-word analysis (Padabhājana) of that term: 'A concordant Saṅgha means those of the same communion (samānasaṃvāsaka) and staying within the same boundary (samānasīmā).' Indeed, a Saṅgha of the same communion is inseparable in mind because of having a common mind. A Saṅgha staying within the same boundary is inseparable in body because of giving bodily concord.

'Should strive for a schism' means making an effort for the purpose of causing a division, thinking, 'How indeed might this Saṅgha be divided?' 'A legal issue (adhikaraṇa) conducive to a schism' means a cause that leads to the objective of dividing the Saṅgha. In this context, 'adhikaraṇa' is intended as 'cause' (kāraṇa), as in the passages 'kāmahetu kāmanidānaṃ kāma-adhikaraṇaṃ' (due to sensual pleasures, having sensual pleasures as the source, on account of sensual pleasures), etc. That cause is of eighteen kinds based on the grounds for causing a schism. 'Having taken up' (samādāya) means having grasped. 'Should persist in supporting' means having grasped that cause which is conducive to a schism and capable of producing a schism in the Saṅgha, one explains it and does not abandon it.

'The bhikkhus should speak to him thus' means that those bhikkhus who see him in person persisting in that support, or those who hear that 'this is happening in such-and-such a monastery,' should speak to him as prescribed in the following words, 'Venerable sir, do not...', even if they have to travel a distance of at least half a yojana. For those who do not speak out despite seeing or hearing it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa). In this context, the word 'mā' (do not) should be connected with the words 'parakkami' (strive) and 'aṭṭhāsi' (persist), as in 'do not strive, do not persist.'

'Let the venerable one be united with the Saṅgha' means let the venerable one join and come together with the Saṅgha; let him be of one view. For what reason? Because a concordant Saṅgha, being in agreement, without disputes, and having a single recitation (of the Pātimokkha), lives happily. In that passage, 'rejoicing' (sammodamāno) means greatly rejoicing through mutual attainment. 'Without disputes' (avivadamāno) means not disputing in this manner: 'This is the Dhamma, this is not the Dhamma.' Having a single recitation of the Pātimokkha performed together is called 'having a single recitation' (ekuddeso). 'Lives happily' (phāsu viharati) means living in comfort.

For one who does not abandon it after being spoken to three times in this way, whether separately or in the midst of the Saṅgha, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa). 'And thus he should be formally admonished' means the act of formal admonition (samanubhāsana-kamma) should be performed. 'This is good' means that such abandoning is beneficial, safe, and a state of well-being for that bhikkhu. If he does not abandon it...
142:
If he abandons it, that is good; if he does not abandon it, he incurs an offense of Saṅghādisesa. In this context, at the conclusion of the formal admonition, there is a Saṅghādisesa for the one who does not abandon it. The meaning of the remaining words is clear.

This training rule was laid down in Rājagaha concerning Devadatta on the occasion of his striving for a schism in the Saṅgha. It is a common rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti) applicable to bhikkhunīs as well. It is a rule where there is no offense by command (anāṇattika). For the bhikkhu who does not abandon it while the formal admonition is being performed, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa) at the end of the motion (ñatti), and two grave offenses (thullaccaya) for the two proclamations (kammavācā). At the end of the third proclamation, which reaches the syllable '-yya' in the phrase 'yassa nakkhamati, so bhāseyya' (whoever does not agree, let him speak), that wrong-doing and those grave offenses are settled, and only the Saṅghādisesa remains. There is no offense for one who is not formally admonished, for one who abandons it, for the insane, and so forth. The four factors here are: lapse in virtue (sīlavipatti), striving for a schism, formal admonition according to the Dhamma, and not abandoning at the conclusion of the proclamation. It has the formal admonition as its source (samanubhāsana-samuṭṭhāna), it is an act of omission (akiriya), it is released by perception (saññāvimokkha), it is intentional (sacittaka), it is a worldly fault (lokavajja), it is an action of body and speech, and it is associated with an unwholesome mind and painful feeling.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Schism in the Saṅgha is finished.

## 11. Bhedānuvattakasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā

In the eleventh training rule, 'of that very one' (tasseva kho pana) means of that very bhikkhu who strives for a schism in the Saṅgha. 'Followers' (anuvattakā) means those who follow by adopting his views, acceptance, and preference. 'Speakers of factionalism' (vaggavādakā) means those who speak words that belong to the side of discord. Because more than three are not eligible for the legal act (since the Saṅgha does not perform a legal act against the Saṅgha), it is said 'one, or two, or three.' 'He knows our [desires]' means he knows our desires and so forth. 'He speaks' means he consults and speaks with us, saying 'Let us do this.' 'This is pleasing to us' means that whatever he does, that action is also pleasing to us. 'Let the venerable ones be united with the Saṅgha' means let the minds of the venerable ones be united with the Saṅgha, let them reach a state of unity. The rest is clear from the meaning of the words. The decision-making discussion here is also just like what was said in the tenth rule.

However, this is the distinction: This training rule was laid down in Rājagaha concerning many bhikkhus who followed Devadatta as he strove for a schism in the Saṅgha. Regarding the factors, just as 'striving' was noted there, 'following' should be noted here.

## The Commentary on the Training Rule on Following the Schismatic is finished.

## 12. Commentary on the Dubbaca Sikkhāpada

In the twelfth, the Dubbaca Sikkhāpada: "Dubbacajātiko" means one who is by nature difficult to admonish, one who is incapable of being spoken to. "Uddesapariyāpannesu" means included or contained within the recitation (uddesa); it refers to the training rules occurring within the Pātimokkha, which are encompassed by the phrase, "If any [monk] has an offense, he should reveal it."

"Sahadhammikaṃ vuccamāno" means being spoken to by means of a training rule practiced by fellow Dhamma-practitioners. Here, the accusative case "sahadhammikaṃ" is used in the sense of the instrumental (cause). It means being spoken to by a training rule prescribed by the Blessed One, which is called "sahadhammika" because it is to be practiced by the five classes of fellow Dhamma-practitioners, or because it belongs to them.

"Viramathāyasmanto mama vacanāya" means: "Venerable sirs, refrain from the speech with which you speak to me; do not speak such words to me."

"Vadatu saha dhammena" means: "Let them speak by means of the training rule of the fellow Dhamma-practitioners, or by means of other words accompanied by the Dhamma that lead to an inspiring state."

The word "yadidaṃ" is a particle used to show the cause of growth. Therefore, it indicates the cause of the growth of the Blessed One's assembly through mutual beneficial speech and mutual lifting up from offenses. The rest is clear in meaning. The decision is similar to what was said in the tenth training rule.

The distinction here is: This training rule was prescribed in Kosambī concerning Venerable Channa, on account of his making himself one who is not to be spoken to (avacanīya). Regarding the factors, just as effort (parakkamana) is seen in that tenth rule, here, the state of being one who is not to be spoken to should be seen.

## The Commentary on the Dubbaca Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 13. Commentary on the Kuladūsaka Sikkhāpada

In the thirteenth, the Kuladūsaka Sikkhāpada: In the phrase "gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā" (a village or a town), a city (nagara) is also included within "village". "Upanissāya viharati" means he lives depending on that [village] because of the connection with requisites such as robes, etc. "Kuladūsaka" (corrupter of families) is one who corrupts families by destroying the faith of people through giving flowers and so on. "Pāpasamācāra" (one of evil conduct) is one who has evil practices such as planting flower bushes and so on. "So bhikkhu" refers to that monk who corrupts families. "Āyasmā..."
144:
...to that monk who corrupts families... "Enough of your staying here"—by this, [the Buddha] shows his worthiness for the act of banishment (pabbājanīyakamma). A monk who has been subjected to the act of banishment is not allowed to wander in the village or town where the act of corrupting families was committed and where he resides, nor is he allowed to stay in that monastery. In the phrase "In this way, that monk," "that" (so) refers to the monk who has been subjected to the act of banishment.

"Chandagāmino" means those who go [astray] because of desire (favoritism); this method applies to the rest [dosa, moha, bhaya]. "That monk" refers to the monk who speaks disparagingly, saying "they go by way of desire," and so on. He should be spoken to for the purpose of relinquishing that speech, not for the purpose of preventing the corruption of families. For, by the act of corrupting families, he has already committed the offenses that were to be committed before the act of banishment. However, if he does not relinquish [that speech] when spoken to either privately or in the midst of the Saṅgha, another dukkaṭa offense is incurred, distinct from the dukkaṭa of corrupting families. The phrase "In this way, that monk" and all other phrases not yet explained before this are clear in meaning. The decision is similar to what was said in the tenth training rule.

The distinction here is: This training rule was prescribed in Sāvatthī concerning the monks Assaji and Punabbhasu, on account of the matter of bringing [the Saṅgha] into [disrepute] through going by way of desire and so on. Regarding the factors, just as effort (parakkamana) is seen in that [tenth rule], here, bringing [into disrepute] (pāpana) through desire and so on should be understood.

## The Commentary on the Kuladūsaka Sikkhāpada is finished.

## Commentary on the Conclusion

In the passage from "Monks, [the thirteen Saṅghādisesa rules] have been recited" to "Thus I bear these in mind": These offenses are called "paṭhamāpattika" (offenses of immediate commission) because they are reached at the very first moment of transgression. Others, however, are to be understood as "yāvatatiyaka" (offenses involving up to the third admonition) because they occur during the formal act of admonition up to the third time, just as a fever that occurs on the third or fourth day is called "tatiyaka" (tertian) or "catutthaka" (quartan).

"Yāvatīhaṃ" means for as many days. "Knowingly conceals" means he hides it while knowing. In that "knowing concealment," the summary (mātikā) of the characteristics of concealment is as follows: 1. It must be an offense, 2. He must perceive it as an offense, 3. He must be a regular monk (pakatatta), 4. He must perceive himself as a regular monk, 5. There must be no obstacles, 6. He must perceive there are no obstacles, 7. He must be able [to reveal it], 8. He must perceive he is able, 9. He must have the desire to conceal, and 10. He must actually conceal it. In that summary, "It must be an offense, and he must perceive it as an offense" means: whatever offense he has committed, it must be one of the thirteen Saṅghādisesas. And that monk, regarding that offense, by way of the basis, [thinks] "This matter for the monks..."
145:
If a monk, even by the mere name of the offense, thinks, 'This is an offense of such a name,' and being aware that it is an offense, intends to conceal it, thinking, 'I will not inform anyone of this offense now,' and thus gives up the responsibility (to report it) and allows the dawn to rise, the offense is considered concealed. However, if in this matter he perceives it as no offense, or perceives it as a different class of offense, or is in doubt, it is considered not concealed.

'Pakatatta' refers to a monk who is not suspended (anukkhitta) and is of common communion (samānasamvāsaka). If such a monk, perceiving himself as one in good standing, conceals the offense in the manner already described, it is considered concealed. 'Anantarāyika' refers to a monk who does not face any of the ten obstacles: kings, thieves, fire, water, humans, non-humans, wild beasts, reptiles, danger to life, and danger to the holy life. If such a monk, perceiving that there are no obstacles, conceals the offense, it is considered concealed. 'Pahū' refers to a monk who is capable of both going to another monk and informing him. If such a monk, perceiving himself as capable, conceals the offense, it is considered concealed.

The two factors—having the desire to conceal and actually concealing—are quite clear. Even if that monk, upon seeing a monk of common communion, does not inform him out of shame, thinking, 'This is my preceptor (upajjhāya) or my teacher (ācariya),' it is still considered concealed. This is because, in the matter of revealing an offense, the status of being a preceptor and so on is not the criterion; only being a person of common communion is the criterion. This is the summary of the decision on the meaning of the phrase 'knowingly conceals.'

'Tāvatīhaṃ' means for as many days. It refers to the duration of time that has passed from the day of concealment until the day of informing, measured in terms of days, fortnights, months, or years. 'Akāmā parivatthabbaṃ' means that one must not live according to one's own will or desire; rather, one must undertake and live the probation (parivāsa) even if it is against one's will.

In that probation, there are three types: probation for concealed offenses (paṭicchanna-parivāsa), purification probation (suddhanta-parivāsa), and combined probation (samodhāna-parivāsa). Among these, the probation for concealed offenses is given in accordance with the offense that was concealed. For some monks, there is an offense concealed for one day; for others, an offense concealed for two days and so on. For some, there is one offense; for others, two, three, or more. Therefore, the Vinaya expert (vinayadhara) who gives the probation for concealed offenses must first know the state of concealment in the manner described, then note the days of concealment and the offenses. If there is one offense concealed for one day, he should have the monk request probation as follows: 'Venerable Sir, I have committed one offense of intentional emission of semen (sañcetanika sukkavissaṭṭhi) concealed for one day.' Then, the probation should be given by reciting the formal act (kammavācā) according to the method found in the Cullavagga Khandhaka. If it was concealed for two or three days...
146:
If the offense was concealed for two days, three days, four days, five days... up to fourteen days, the application should be made according to the number of days. For an offense concealed for fifteen days, the application should be made as 'concealed for a fortnight' (pakkhappaticchanna).

From those fifteen days up to the twenty-ninth day, it should be applied as 'concealed for more than a fortnight.' Thereafter, the application should be made as: concealed for one month, concealed for more than a month, concealed for two months, concealed for more than two months, concealed for three months... up to concealed for more than eleven months. When one year is completed, it should be applied as 'concealed for one year.' Thereafter, it should be applied as: concealed for more than a year, concealed for two years, and so on up to concealed for sixty years, or concealed for more than sixty years, or even longer than that.

If there are two, three, or more offenses, just as it was said 'one offense,' it should be said 'two offenses' or 'three offenses.' Beyond that, whether it be a hundred or a thousand, it is allowable to say 'many offenses' (sambahulā).

In the case of offenses with various bases (vatthu), the application can be made by way of count: 'Venerable Sir, I have committed many saṅghādisesa offenses concealed for one day: one sukkavissaṭṭhi, one kāyasaṃsagga, one duṭṭhullavācā, one attakāma, and one sañcaritta.' Or, it can be made by way of specifying the bases: 'Venerable Sir, I have committed many saṅghādisesa offenses of various bases concealed for one day.' Or, it can be made by way of the mere name: 'Venerable Sir, I have committed many saṅghādisesa offenses concealed for one day.'

In that context (of applying by mere name), the name is of two kinds: common to the same class (sajātisaadhāraṇa) and common to all (sabbasaadhāraṇa). Among these, the name 'saṅghādisesa' is common to the same class, and the name 'āpatti' (offense) is common to all. Therefore, it is also allowable to speak by way of the name common to all, such as: 'I have committed many offenses concealed for one day.'

Indeed, this disciplinary act (vinayakamma) of probation and so on is allowable to be performed by way of the basis (vatthu), the lineage (gotta), the name (nāma), or the offense (āpatti). Among these, the name 'sukkavissaṭṭhi' is considered both a basis and a lineage. The name 'saṅghādisesa' is considered both a name and an offense. Thus, by the words 'sukkavissaṭṭhi, kāyasaṃsagga,' etc., as well as by the words 'offenses of various bases' (nānāvatthukāyo), the basis and the lineage are included. By the word 'saṅghādisesa' as well as by the word 'offenses' (āpattiyo), the name and the offense are included. Therefore, the formal act (kammavācā) should be performed by way of any one of these.
147:
At the conclusion of the kammavācā, if it is a monastery with few monks and one can stay without incurring a break in the nights (ratticcheda), one should undertake the duties (vatta) three times in that very place where the probation (parivāsa) was granted, saying: "I undertake the probation (parivāsa), I undertake the duties (vatta)." Having undertaken them, one should inform the Saṅgha in that same place and also inform any monks who arrive later, and live under probation without causing a breach of the duties (vattabheda) or a break in the nights.

If it is not possible to clear the probation (without breach of duty) and one wishes to stay having relinquished the duties, the probation should be relinquished in the midst of the Saṅgha or in the presence of a single individual, saying: "I relinquish the probation, I relinquish the duties." In this matter, even if relinquished with a single phrase, the probation is relinquished; however, relinquishing with both phrases is more firm. The same method applies to the undertaking (samādāna). From the time of relinquishment, he stands in the status of a regular monk (pakatatta). Then, at the time of dawn, together with one monk, he should go beyond a distance of about two stone-throws from the enclosure of a fenced monastery, or from a place suitable for an enclosure in an unfenced monastery, stepping off the main road and sitting in a place concealed by a thicket or a fence; there, before the rising of the dawn (aruṇa), he should undertake the duties and inform (the other monk). He must also inform any other monk he sees. When the dawn has risen, he should relinquish the duties in the presence of that monk and return to the monastery. If that companion monk has left for some business before dawn, he should go to the monastery and relinquish the duties after informing the very first monk he encounters. Having noted this, he should live under probation until the number of nights is completed. This is the decision regarding the Paṭicchanna-parivāsa (Probation for Concealed Offenses) in brief. The details should be understood according to the method stated in the Samantapāsādikā, the Vinaya Commentary (Cūḷavagga Commentary 97).

Regarding the remaining two, the probation authorized in the Cūḷavagga Khandhaka in the case of "not knowing the limit of the offenses, not knowing the limit of the nights" (Cūḷavagga 157) is called Suddhanta-parivāsa (Complete Purification Probation). That Suddhanta-parivāsa is of two kinds: Cūḷasuddhanta and Mahāsuddhanta. Both kinds are given to a monk who does not know, does not remember, or is doubtful about the entire limit of the nights or a part of it. As for the limit of the offenses, whether he knows "I have committed this many offenses" or not, that knowledge or lack thereof is not the reason. The procedure for giving that Suddhanta-parivāsa has come in the Khandhaka. The decision, however, is stated in detail in the Samantapāsādikā (Cūḷavagga Commentary 102). The other kind is called Samodhāna-parivāsa (Combined Probation). It is of three kinds:
148:
Odhāna-samodhāna, Aggha-samodhāna, and Missaka-samodhāna. Among these three, Odhāna-samodhāna refers to the probation given to a monk who, having committed intervening offenses and concealed them, has the days he already lived under probation set aside and discarded, and the later offense is combined with the original limit of days of the previous offense. Aggha-samodhāna refers to the probation given for many offenses where one, two, three, or many offenses have been concealed for the longest time; by combining them according to their value (duration), the probation is given based on the limit of nights of those offenses for the remaining offenses that were concealed for a shorter time. Missaka-samodhāna refers to the probation given by combining offenses of various grounds (vatthu) into one. This is the brief discussion on all three types of Samodhāna-parivāsa. The details are stated in the Samantapāsādikā (Cūḷavagga Commentary 102). This is the introduction to the decision on the word "parivatthabba" (should live under probation).

"Uttari cha-rattā" means for six nights beyond the probation. "Bhikkhu-mānattāya" means for the state of being revered by monks, or for the purpose of pleasing (the Saṅgha). "Paṭipajjitabbaṃ" means it should be practiced. This bhikkhu-mānatta is also of two kinds: according to whether it is concealed or unconcealed. Among those two, for a monk who has an unconcealed offense, mānatta alone is given without giving parivāsa; this is Appaṭicchanna-mānatta. The mānatta given at the end of the probation for a monk who has a concealed offense is called Paṭicchanna-mānatta; here, it is this Paṭicchanna-mānatta that is intended. The procedure for giving both these types of mānatta and the decision should be understood according to the method stated in the Samantapāsādikā (Cūḷavagga Commentary 102); here, it is only a summary. If this monk practicing mānatta relinquishes the duties and goes to undertake them at dawn, he should go to the place mentioned in the section on parivāsa together with at least four monks, undertake them saying, "I undertake the mānatta, I undertake the duties," and after informing them, whether those monks have left or not, he should practice according to the previous method.

In the phrase "Yattha siyā vīsati-gaṇo," it is called vīsati-gaṇo because there is a group (gaṇa) of a Saṅgha of twenty. "Tatra" means in that precinct (sīmā) where there is a Bhikkhu-saṅgha of at least a group of twenty. "Abbhetabbo" means he should be accepted, he should be restored to the Saṅgha by means of the act of rehabilitation (abbhāna-kamma). Or it means he should be called back. The act of rehabilitation is stated according to the Pāḷi in the Khandhaka (Cūḷavagga 100 etc.) and according to the decision in the Samantapāsādikā. "Anabbhito" means not accepted, one for whom the act of rehabilitation has not been performed. Or it means one who has not been called back. "Those monks are also blameworthy" refers to those monks who (knowing the deficiency of being fewer than twenty, accept him).
149: Knowing (the fact that the number is less than twenty), they perform the abbhāna (rehabilitation); those monks are also to be censured, and they incur a Dukkaṭa offense along with a fault that is greatly to be regretted. "Ayaṃ tattha sāmīcī" means that what has been stated is the proper practice, the instruction and advice following the nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma), and the custom in accordance with the supramundane states. The remaining words in this concluding sentence are just as previously explained. ## In the Explanation of the Pātimokkha called Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī, ## The Explanation of the Saṅghādisesa is finished. In the section on the Indeterminate (Aniyata) rules, the sentence beginning with "Ime kho pana" is just as previously explained. "Mātugāmena" refers to a human female who is still alive, even if she was born on that very day. "Eko ekāya" means a single monk together with a single woman called a mātugāma. "Raho" means in a secluded place, out of sight. Although "out of hearing" appears in the Pāḷi text, in this training rule, "raho" is intended only as "out of sight."
151:
At Sāvatthī, the first Indefinite training rule was laid down concerning the Elder Udāyī, regarding the matter of sitting with a woman in the aforementioned type of seat. It is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇa-paññatti) and is a regulation not by command (anāṇattika). A Dukkaṭa offense is incurred for all preliminary efforts, starting from the application of eye-salve and so on, because of the desire to go to the presence of a woman for secret enjoyment, which is the defilement based on sexual intercourse. After going there, if the woman sits while the monk is sitting, or the monk sits while the woman is sitting, or both sit simultaneously without one being before or after the other, a Pācittiya offense is incurred due to the sitting of both. If, however, he commits physical contact (kāyasaṃsaggā) or sexual intercourse, he is to be dealt with according to those acts. In the case of lying down, the method is the same.

When a sighted, wise man as described before is within the vicinity (upacāra) of twelve cubits and is not asleep, there is no offense for a monk who is standing, or for a monk who does not care for seclusion (arahopekkha), or for one whose mind is occupied elsewhere, on account of sitting. For those who are insane and so on, there is no offense regarding all three types of offenses. In some cases, it may be a failure in virtue (sīla-vipatti), and in others, a failure in conduct (ācāra-vipatti). Whichever offense he acknowledges, the distinction of the factors (anga) should be known by that acknowledgment. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so on are exactly like the first Pārājika.

## The Explanation of the First Indefinite Training Rule Ends.

## 2. Explanation of the Second Indefinite Training Rule

In the second Indefinite training rule, any wise person, whether a woman or a man, who is not blind and not deaf, and is standing or sitting within twelve cubits, can prevent the offense even if they are distracted or drowsy. However, a deaf person, even if sighted, or a blind person, even if not deaf, cannot prevent the offense. The distinction here is that, excluding the Pārājika offense, the offense of lewd words (duṭṭhullavācā) is mentioned. The rest is to be understood in the same manner as the previous rule. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so on in this rule are exactly like Adinnādāna (theft).

## The Explanation of the Second Indefinite Training Rule Ends.

The concluding words beginning with "Uddiṭṭhā kho" are to be understood in all places according to the method already stated.

152:
## Nissaggiya Chapter
From here onwards, it should be understood in the same manner as previously stated everywhere, starting with "Ime kho pana," etc.

## 1. Robe Chapter

## 1. Commentary on the Kathina Training Rule
Among the Nissaggiya training rules, in the first training rule of the Robe Chapter, "when the robe is finished" (niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ) means either by the completion of the sewing work, or when the robe matter is finished through any of these four ways: "the robe is lost, destroyed, burnt, or the expectation of obtaining a robe is cut off." This means the impediment (palibodha) regarding the making of the robe is cut off. Indeed, for a monk who has spread the Kathina, as long as the robe-impediment is not cut off by these means, he receives the Kathina benefits. "When the Kathina is removed" (ubbhatasmiṃ kathine) refers to when that Kathina spread by the Saṅgha has been removed. In this regard, the spreading of the Kathina and the removal of the Kathina should be understood in brief.

This spreading of the Kathina was allowed by the Blessed One for monks who have completed the first rainy season retreat (purimavassa). This spreading of the Kathina is valid only if there is a minimum of five persons. Therefore, in a monastery where there are only four, three, two, or one monk who entered the first rainy season retreat, it should be spread by including monks who entered the later rainy season retreat (pacchimavassa) to complete the group (gaṇapūraka). Those who complete the group only serve to fulfill the number and do not receive the Kathina benefits. Therefore, if a layperson or any monk legally and rightfully offers a robe to the monks who have completed the first rainy season retreat, saying, "Please spread the Kathina with this robe," that robe should be given to the monk worthy of spreading the Kathina by the formal act with a motion and a second (ñattidutiya-kammavācā) as taught in the Khandhaka.

That monk who spreads the Kathina must, on that very day, cut the cloth into five or more segments and make either an outer robe (saṅghāṭi), an upper robe (uttarāsaṅga), or an inner robe (antaravāsaka). The remaining monks should also assist him as companions. If a robe that is already sewn and dyed is obtained, that is even better. However, it is not allowable to spread the Kathina with cloth that is uncut or unsewn. If that monk who is to spread the Kathina wishes to spread it with the outer robe, he should relinquish (paccuddharaṇa) the old outer robe, determine (adhiṭṭhāna) the new outer robe, and then spread it by saying, "I spread the Kathina with this outer robe." The same method applies to the upper robe and the inner robe.

After spreading it in this way, that monk should approach the monks who have completed the first rainy season retreat and are within the boundary (sīmā) and say, "Venerable sirs, the Kathina of the Saṅgha has been spread; the spreading of the Kathina is according to the Dhamma; please rejoice." To the elders, the juniors, the many, or to each individual, he should speak appropriately...
153:
...having noted [the seniority], he should speak. Those monks who rejoice should also say, "Venerable sir, the Kathina of the Saṅgha has been spread," or "Friend, the Kathina of the Saṅgha has been spread," and then say, "The spreading of the Kathina is according to the Dhamma; we rejoice," or "I rejoice." Among the monks who completed the first rainy season retreat, the Kathina is considered spread only for those who rejoice. From that time of rejoicing until the removal of the Kathina, they receive these five benefits: wandering without having asked permission (anāmantacāra), wandering without taking the triple robe (asamādānacāra), keeping robes as long as one wishes (yāvadatthacīvara), a group meal (gaṇabhojana), and whatever robes arise there, as well as robes arising for the Saṅgha in that monastery. This is the spreading of the Kathina.

That Kathina, however, is removed by means of any one of the eight grounds (mātikā) taught as follows: "Monks, there are these eight grounds for the removal of the Kathina: the ground of departure, the ground of completion, the ground of resolve, the ground of loss, the ground of hearing, the ground of the cutting off of expectation, the ground of crossing the boundary, and the ground of simultaneous removal." The detailed decision on this should be understood according to the method stated in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary. Thus, by the phrase "when the Kathina is removed," it shows the absence of the remaining impediment.

"Ten days at most" (dasāhaparamanti) means ten days is the maximum limit; the meaning is that it can be kept for a period having ten days as its maximum limit. A robe that is extra because it is not included among those determined (adhiṭṭhita) or shared (vikappita) is called an extra robe (atirekacīvara). A "robe" is any one of these six types: linen, cotton, silk, wool, hemp, and cloth mixed with these five, or any one of those that are similar to these six. This is its type. In terms of size, however, the smallest robe suitable for sharing (vikappana) is intended in this training rule. In this regard, it has been said: "Monks, I allow the sharing of the smallest robe, which is eight finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in width, by the Sugata's finger-breadth."

In the phrase "because it is not included among those determined or shared," the status of what should be determined and what should be shared should be understood by this method: "Monks, I allow the triple robe to be determined, not shared; the rain-cloth to be determined for the four months of the rainy season, and after that, I allow it to be shared; the sitting cloth to be determined, not shared; the bedding to be determined, not shared; the itch-cloth to be determined as long as the illness lasts, and after that, I allow it to be shared; the face towel to be determined, not shared; the requisite cloth to be determined, not shared." Among these [nine] types of cloth, a monk who wishes to determine the triple robe should determine only a robe of proper size after it has been dyed and marked with a proper mark (kappabindu). Regarding the size of that robe, a size smaller than the Sugata's robe is suitable as the maximum limit. As for the minimum limit, for the outer robe and the upper robe, a size of five cubits in length and three cubits in width is suitable.
154:
The length of the uttarāsaṅga (upper robe) should be five hand-spans (muṭṭhi), and the width should be three hand-spans. The antaravāsaka (inner robe) is five hand-spans in length, and it is also allowable if the width is two cubits. Any robe that exceeds or falls short of the aforementioned measurements must be determined as a 'parikkhāracola' (accessory cloth).

Regarding the method of determination: Since the Buddha taught that 'there are two ways to determine a robe: by body or by speech,' one should first withdraw the determination of the old saṅghāṭi (outer robe) by saying, 'I withdraw this saṅghāṭi.' Then, holding the new one with the hand, one should determine it by body (through a physical gesture while mentally intending 'I determine this saṅghāṭi') or by speech (by vocalizing the words). There are two ways of vocal determination: if the robe is within arm's reach (hatthapāsa), one should vocalize, 'I determine this saṅghāṭi.' If it is inside a room or a nearby monastery, one should note its location and vocalize, 'I determine that saṅghāṭi.'

The same method applies to the uttarāsaṅga and antaravāsaka; the only difference is the name. Therefore, all robes must be determined by their respective names: saṅghāṭi, uttarāsaṅga, or antaravāsaka. If one makes a saṅghāṭi, etc., from cloth that has already been determined, once the dyeing and the marking (kappabindu) are finished, one must withdraw the determination of the cloth by saying, 'I withdraw this cloth,' and then re-determine it. This triple robe (ticīvara) may also be determined as parikkhāracola for the sake of easy use.

The rain-cloth (vassikasāṭikā), if it does not exceed the standard size, should be determined by name for the four months of the rainy season according to the method already mentioned. After those four months, the determination should be withdrawn and it should be assigned (vikappana). It is allowable even if it is dyed just enough to change the color, but having two is not allowed. The sitting cloth (nisīdana) should also be determined according to the method mentioned; it must be of the correct size and only one is allowed; two are not allowed. The floor covering (paccattharaṇa) must also be determined; whether large, single, or many, they are allowable. Various types such as blue, yellow, fringed, or floral-fringed coverings are all allowable.

The itch-covering cloth (kaṇḍuppaṭicchādi) should be determined according to size for as long as the ailment lasts. When the ailment is cured, the determination should be withdrawn and it should be assigned. Only one such cloth is allowed. The face towel (mukhapuñchanacola) must also be determined; whether one, many, or large, it is allowable. There is no limit to the number of accessory cloths (parikkhāracola); one may determine as many as desired. Bags (thavikā) and water filters (parissāvana) of at least the minimum size for assignment should be determined as 'parikkhāracola.' Many items can be determined together by saying, 'I determine these robes as accessory cloths.' Bolsters for beds and chairs...
155:
Regarding bolsters for beds and chairs, pillows, blankets, and carpets given for the purpose of lodging accessories (senāsana-parikkhāra), there is no need for formal determination. All robes determined in the aforementioned manner lose their determination through these eight causes: giving it to another, it being snatched away, it being taken on trust, returning to the lay life, renouncing the training, death, change of gender, or withdrawal of determination (paccuddharaṇa). The determination of the triple robe (ticīvara) is also lost if there is a hole the size of the back of the nail of the little finger, provided it is a hole that goes all the way through. If even a single thread remains unbroken within the hole, the determination is preserved. Among the triple robes, in the saṅghāṭi and uttarāsaṅga, a hole within one span from the long edge or eight finger-breadths from the short edge breaks the determination. In the antaravāsaka, it is the same distance from the long edge, but four finger-breadths from the short edge. A hole outside these specified areas in any of the three robes does not break the determination. Therefore, when such a hole occurs, the triple robe becomes an 'extra robe' (atireka-cīvara). After repairing it, it must be determined again. The determination of the rain-cloth is lost when the rainy months pass, and the itch-covering cloth when the ailment is cured. Therefore, they should be assigned (vikappana) after that time. The characteristics of assignment for all robes will be explained in the Vikappana Sikkhāpada. In the context of this training rule, a robe that is neither determined nor assigned is known as an 'extra robe' (atireka-cīvara).

'For one who lets it exceed [ten days], there is an offense of forfeiture and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya)': this means if a monk keeps a robe of the specified type and size for more than ten days without making it not an extra robe (by determination or assignment) within those ten days, he commits a nissaggiya pācittiya offense. The robe becomes forfeitable, and the monk incurs a pācittiya offense. Alternatively, 'Nissaggiya' means forfeiture (nissajjana). This is the name of the Vinaya procedure to be performed before the confession of the offense. Because it involves the procedure of forfeiture, it is called 'nissaggiya.' What is it? It is a pācittiya. For one who exceeds the time, there is a pācittiya offense accompanied by the Vinaya procedure of forfeiture; this is the meaning in this second method. This forfeitable robe is reckoned from the day it was obtained; the dawn that follows belongs to the day of acquisition. Therefore, including the day of acquisition, at the eleventh dawn, ten days have been exceeded. One must take that robe and forfeit it to the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual. The method for forfeiting to the Saṅgha is as follows: 'Venerable sirs, this robe of mine, having exceeded ten days, is forfeitable. I forfeit it to the Saṅgha.' After forfeiting, one should confess the offense: 'Venerable sirs, I have fallen into a nissaggiya pācittiya offense.'
156:
"I confess it"—in this way, the offense should be confessed. If there are two offenses, one should say "two"; if more than that, one should say "many offenses." In the case of forfeiture as well, if there are two or many [robes], one should say: "Venerable sirs, these robes of mine, having exceeded ten days, are to be forfeited. I forfeit these robes to the Saṅgha." If one is unable to say it in Pali, it may be said in another language.

A clever and able monk should inform the Saṅgha: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. This monk named so-and-so remembers, reveals, makes manifest, and confesses an offense. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, I shall receive the offense of the monk named so-and-so." Having received the offense in this manner, he should ask: "Do you see [the offense]?" [The other] should reply: "Yes, I see it." When he says: "In the future, you should be restrained," [the other] should say: "Very well, I will be well restrained." In the case of two offenses or many offenses, the change in grammatical number should be made according to the previous method.

After the offense has been confessed, the forfeited robe should be returned thus: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. This Nissaggiya robe of the monk named so-and-so has been forfeited to the Saṅgha. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha give this robe back to the monk named so-and-so." If there are two or many [robes], the change in grammatical number should be made.

A monk wishing to forfeit to a group (gaṇa) should say "this robe" or "these robes" and say: "I forfeit [them] to the venerable ones." The monk receiving the offense should also announce: "Venerable ones, let the venerable ones hear me. This monk named so-and-so remembers... (pe)... confesses an offense. If it is suitable for the venerable ones..." In returning the robe as well, he should say: "Venerable ones, let the venerable ones hear me. This Nissaggiya robe of the monk named so-and-so has been forfeited to the venerable ones. If it is suitable for the venerable ones, let the venerable ones give this robe back to the monk named so-and-so." The rest of the procedure is the same as the previous method.

A monk wishing to forfeit to an individual (puggala) should say "this robe" or "these robes" and say: "I forfeit [them] to the venerable one." After forfeiting, he should confess the offense thus: "Venerable sir, I have fallen into a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense; I confess it." If [the recipient] is junior, he should say: "Friend (Āvuso)." If the monk receiving the confession says: "Do you see?" or "Do you [plural] see?", he should say: "Yes, venerable sir" or "Yes, friend," and say: "I see it." Then, if he says: "In the future, you should be restrained" or "You [plural] should be restrained," he should say: "Very well, I will be well restrained." After confessing the offense in this way, [the robe] should be returned by saying: "I give this robe to the venerable one." In the case of two...
157:
In the case of three offenses or three robes, the procedure should be understood according to the method previously stated. In forfeiting to two monks, it should be forfeited as if to a group. Thereafter, the receiving of the offense and the returning of the forfeited robe should be performed by one of those two as if by a single individual. This is the procedure for all Nissaggiyas. The difference is only in the objects, such as robe, bowl, or sitting mat. For an object not present (in front of the monk), it should be forfeited by saying: "this object." If there are many, one should say: "these objects." The same method applies to returning the forfeited object. For a monk who, perceiving "this object has been given to me by this monk," does not return the forfeited object, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). A monk who, knowing it is the owner's property, takes it by some pretext, should be made to settle it by having the goods valued upon the owner's relinquishing of responsibility.

The rule was laid down in Vesālī concerning the group of six monks regarding the matter of wearing an extra robe. "Ten days at most" is the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) in this rule. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti). It is an offense not by command (anāṇattika). For a monk who uses it without forfeiting, there is an offense of wrongdoing. As in this rule, so it is in all rules. Therefore, we shall not mention that wrongdoing later. For a monk who perceives it as exceeded when ten days have not yet passed, or who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrongdoing. When it has exceeded [ten days], for a monk who perceives it as exceeded, or who perceives it as not exceeded, or who is in doubt, there is only an offense of Nissaggiya Pācittiya. Likewise, for robes that are not determined, not assigned, not abandoned, not lost, not destroyed, not burnt, and not stolen, if a monk perceives them as determined, etc., [the offense is the same]. There is no offense for robes that, within ten days, are determined, assigned, abandoned, lost, destroyed, burnt, stolen, or taken in trust, nor for insane persons and the like.

This training rule is a failure in conduct (ācāra-vipatti). Like this rule, the rules following this are also failures in conduct. In both Pātimokkhas (of monks and nuns), Pārājika offenses and Saṅghādisesa offenses are failures in virtue (sīla-vipatti). The remaining offenses are failures in conduct. There is no offense called failure in livelihood (ājīva-vipatti) or failure in view (diṭṭhi-vipatti). However, based on failure in livelihood, excluding the Dubbhāsita, six classes of offenses are laid down. Based on failure in view, two classes of offenses are laid down: Pācittiya and Dukkaṭa. This is the definition here. Thus, the discussion on failure (vipatti-kathā) ends here. Therefore, we shall not examine that discussion on failure after this. The five factors here are: the robe being of proper kind and size, being one's own property, being counted [as extra], the connection (palibodha) being severed, being an extra robe, and exceeding ten days. The origins are: Kathina-samuṭṭhāna, akiriya (omission), no-saññā-vimokkha (not released by perception), acittaka (regardless of intention), paṇṇatti-vajja (prohibited by regulation), bodily action, vocal action, three thoughts, and three feelings.

## The Explanation of the Kathina Training Rule is Finished.
158:
## 2. Commentary on the Udosite Training Rule

In the second training rule, regarding the phrase "niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunā," the meaning should not be taken as in the previous training rule; rather, the instrumental case (nā) should be understood in the sense of the possessive case (of), as in "when the monk's robe is finished." This is because, in the sense of the instrumental case, there is no specific action to be performed, such as "the monk must do such and such a task." However, in the sense of the possessive case, it is appropriate to interpret it as: when the monk's robe is finished and the Kathina has been withdrawn, and thus the attachment (palibodha) is severed by these two—the completion of the robe and the withdrawal of the Kathina—if the monk stays apart from the triple robe (ti-cīvara) for even one night.

In that context, "ti-cīverena" (with the triple robe) refers to being apart from any one of the three robes, such as the outer robe (saṅghāṭī), which have been formally determined according to the method of determining the triple robe. "Vippavaseyya" means to stay separated. In the Pāli, it is taught as "a village has a single precinct, or various precincts," etc. This refers to leaving the robe in any of the fifteen types of storage places—village, market town, house, storehouse (udosite), watchtower, hall, palace, brick building, boat, caravan, field, threshing floor, park, monastery, or at the foot of a tree, or in an open space—and allowing the dawn to rise while being in a place beyond the reach (hatthapāsa) of that village and so on. This is the summary; the detailed explanation has already been given in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary.

"Aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā" means: except for the "authorization for staying apart from the triple robe" which the Saṅgha grants to a sick monk. It should be understood that for a monk who has not received such authorization, if he stays apart for even one night, he incurs a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense as previously mentioned. In this training rule, the only distinction is the difference in the formula for forfeiture, such as: "Venerable sir, this robe of mine, which I have stayed apart from at night without the authorization of the monks, is to be forfeited."

## It was laid down in Sāvatthī regarding many monks who set out on a journey to the countryside with only an undergarment and an upper garment.

"Aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā" is the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) of this training rule. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti) and a rule without a specific command (anāṇattika). For one who perceives a robe from which he must not stay apart as one from which he may stay apart, or who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). For one who perceives a robe from which he must stay apart as one from which he may stay apart, or as one from which he must not stay apart, or who is in doubt, there is a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense. Likewise, if one perceives robes that have not been revoked (paccuddhaṭa) or relinquished as being revoked or relinquished, an offense is incurred.

There is no offense if the robe is revoked before dawn, or in the cases of relinquishment mentioned in the first Kathina training rule. Likewise, there is no offense for a monk who has received authorization to stay apart. When the illness is cured, he must return to where the robe is, or revoke it while staying right there. However, if that same illness or another illness recurs, the authorization already received remains valid.
159:
The four factors here are: the robe being determined (adhiṭṭhita), the Kathina not being spread, the authorization not being received, and staying apart at night. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so on are exactly as described in the first Kathina training rule. However, in that first Kathina training rule, the failure to determine or assign (vikappanā) is an omission (akiriya), whereas in this training rule, the failure to revoke (paccuddharaṇa) is the omission. This is the distinction.

## The Commentary on the Udosite Training Rule is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Akālacīvara Training Rule

In the third rule, in the phrase "niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunā," (the word bhikkhunā) should also be understood in the possessive sense. "Out-of-season robe" (akālacīvara) refers to a robe that arises at a time other than the robe-season, which is defined as "the last month of the rainy season (Tazaungmon) if the Kathina is not spread, or five months if the Kathina is spread." Furthermore, even if it is within the robe-season, a robe given to the Saṅgha with the words "This is an out-of-season robe," or to an individual with the words "I give this robe to you," is also called an out-of-season robe.

"Uppajjeyya" (should arise) means obtaining such a robe through one's share from the Saṅgha, or from a group such as Suttanta reciters, or from relatives, or from friends, or as a rag-robe (paṃsukūla), or by means of one's own wealth. Alternatively, it means arising from any one of the eight grounds (mātikā) for the arising of robes: "Monks, there are eight grounds for the arising of robes: giving at the boundary (sīmā), giving by agreement, giving at the place of alms-food, giving to the Saṅgha, giving to both Saṅghas, giving to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains, giving by designation, and giving to an individual." In this context, one who gives by referring to the boundary, saying "I give at the boundary," is said to give at the boundary. This method applies similarly to all the grounds.

In this context, there are fifteen types of boundaries (sīmā): the small boundary (khaṇḍasīmā), the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā), the boundary of common affiliation, the boundary of not staying apart, the boundary of gains, the village boundary, the market town boundary, the city boundary, the interior boundary (abbhantara), the water boundary (udakukkhepa), the countryside boundary, the country boundary (raṭṭha), the royal capital boundary (rajja), the island boundary, and the universe boundary. Among these, the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā) refers to the area demarcated by the fence in a fenced monastery, or the area that ought to be fenced in an unfenced monastery. Alternatively, it should be understood as the "precinct boundary" within two stone-throws (leḍḍupāta) by a man of average strength from the monks' regular assembly point, or from the outermost dining hall, or from the regular living quarters. That precinct boundary expands as the monastery grows and contracts as it diminishes.
160:
If the monastery declines, the precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā) also declines; even up to a hundred yojanas, it remains only the precinct boundary. Gains given within that precinct boundary reach all monks who have entered within the boundary. All procedures such as bhikkhunīs entering the monastery, requesting permission for lodgings, informing about the practice of parivāsa and mānatta, the interruption of the rains-retreat, taking dependence (nissaya), and accepting monastery lodgings should be understood as being by the power of this precinct boundary.

Regarding the revenue boundary (lābha-sīmā): when kings, royal ministers, and others have a monastery built and demarcate an area of one gāvuta, half a yojana, or one yojana around it, saying, "This is the revenue boundary of our monastery; whatever taxes, grain, etc., arise within this area, we donate them to our monastery," such a designated area is called a lābha-sīmā.

Within countries such as Kāsi and Kosala, there are many districts (janapada). There, the demarcation of a single district is a janapada-sīmā; the demarcation of a country like Kāsi or Kosala is a raṭṭha-sīmā; the area where a king's authority extends is a rajja-sīmā; a large or small island bounded by the ocean is a dīpa-sīmā; and the interior area enclosed by the Cakkavāḷa mountains is a cakkavāḷa-sīmā. The nature of the remaining boundaries should be understood according to the method already stated in the Nidānakathā.

Among those boundaries, an item offered with the words "I give to the khaṇḍa-sīmā" reaches only the monks within that khaṇḍa-sīmā; it does not reach monks in the sīmantarika (the space between boundaries) outside of it. However, an item offered with the words "I give to the upacāra-sīmā" reaches monks situated in the khaṇḍa-sīmā and the sīmantarika, which are within that demarcation. An item offered to a samānasamvāsaka-sīmā (great boundary) does not reach monks in the khaṇḍa-sīmā and sīmantarika. An item offered to an avippavāsa-sīmā and a lābha-sīmā reaches only those included within those boundaries. An item offered to a gāma-sīmā (village boundary) and so on reaches monks in the baddha-sīmā (consecrated boundary) within those boundaries as well. An item offered to an abbhantara-sīmā and an udakukkhepa-sīmā (water boundary) reaches only those included within them. An item offered to a janapada-sīmā and so on also reaches monks in the baddha-sīmā within them.

Therefore, if someone staying in Jambudīpa makes an offering saying, "I give to the Saṅgha in the island of Tambapaṇṇi (Sri Lanka)," a single monk from Tambapaṇṇi may come and accept it on behalf of all. If a monk from Tambapaṇṇi who is already in Jambudīpa takes the share for his fellow monks, it should not be forbidden. If a donor enters a monastery and says simply, "I give to the sīmā," without specifying a particular boundary, he should be asked, "There are many kinds of boundaries; which boundary do you intend?" If he says, "I do not know these distinctions; let the Saṅgha residing in the sīmā take it," then it should be distributed by the monks residing in the upacāra-sīmā.

In the word "katikāya," a katikā is an agreement made to equalize gains. That agreement should be made in this way: the monks assembled in one monastery, wishing to support another monastery and desiring to equalize gains, should mention the name of that monastery and say, "Such-and-such a monastery is old and has few gains" (and then ask the Saṅgha if they agree to make the gains of that monastery equal to this one).
161:
Having stated some reason, one should announce three times: "Does the Saṅgha approve of making that monastery have equal gains with this monastery?" By this much, a monk residing in that monastery is considered as one residing in this monastery. The same should be done in that monastery as well; by doing so, a monk residing in this monastery is considered as one residing in that monastery. When gains are distributed in one monastery, it is proper to take a share for a monk residing in the other monastery.

Regarding the term "bhikkhā-paññatti," it refers to the place (monastery) designated by the donor for the distribution of their relinquished property. Therefore, if it is said, "I give to the monastery where my regular meritorious deeds are performed," or "Give to that monastery," then whether it is where the donor's regular meal-offering is prepared, or where they constantly feed the monks, or where they have built some lodging, it is considered given in all those places. However, if there are very few monks at a place of regular meritorious deeds, or if there is only a single robe, it should be summarized (mātikā) and taken according to what the donor says.

Regarding the phrase "gives to the Saṅgha," an item offered by entering a monastery and saying, "I give to the Saṅgha," reaches the monks who have arrived at the upacāra-sīmā, as well as those who are outside the upacāra-sīmā but are physically connected (in a continuous line) with those monks. Therefore, if there is someone to accept on their behalf, the shares should be given even to the monks who have not yet arrived. An item offered upon seeing monks outside the upacāra-sīmā with the words "to the Saṅgha" reaches the assembly that is physically connected. However, it does not reach monks who have not reached the assembly within twelve cubits.

Regarding the phrase "to the Ubhato-saṅgha" (to both Saṅghas), half of the item offered to the Ubhato-saṅgha should be given to the monks and half to the nuns. Even if there is only one monk or one nun, or even just an unordained person (novice), only half should be given. If it is said, "To the Ubhato-saṅgha and to you," and if there are ten monks and ten nuns, twenty-one shares should be made: one share is given to the individual, ten shares to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, and ten shares to the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha. The individual who receives a personal share is also entitled to take a share from the Saṅgha according to his seniority (vassagga). Why? Because he is included in the term "Ubhato-saṅgha." The same method applies when it is said, "To the Ubhato-saṅgha and to the cetiya (shrine)." However, in this case, there is no such thing as a share reaching the cetiya from the Saṅgha; there is only one share equal to the share received by a single individual. If it is said, "To the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and to the nuns," it should not be divided in the middle; rather, it should be given by counting the monks and the nuns. If it is said, "To the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, to the nuns, and to you," the individual does not receive a separate share, but receives only one share from the portion that reaches him...
162:
One receives it. However, if it is said, "And for the shrine" (cetiyassa ca), one individual's share is obtained for the shrine. Even if it is said, "And for the monks and for the nuns" (bhikkhūnañca bhikkhunīnañca), it should not be divided in the middle but should be distributed according to the number of individuals. The consideration of the individual and the shrine together with them is just as the method previously mentioned. Just as the method was derived starting with the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, it should also be derived starting with the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. If it is said, "And for the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and for you" (bhikkhusaṅghassa ca tuyhañca), it cannot be obtained separately for the individual, but it is obtained for the shrine. Even if it is said, "And for the monks and for you" (bhikkhūnañca tuyhañca), it cannot be obtained separately, but it is indeed obtained for the shrine.

Regarding the term "For the Saṅgha that has completed the rains-retreat" (vassaṃvuttha-saṅghassa): If one enters a monastery and says, "I give to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains-retreat," those monks who completed the first rains-retreat (purimavassa) in that monastery without interruption receive it, even if they are standing outside the boundary (sīmā); others do not. However, if one stands outside the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā) and says, "To the Saṅgha that has completed the rains-retreat," all those who have completed the rains-retreat and have arrived from anywhere receive it. If one says, "To the Saṅgha that has completed the rains-retreat in such-and-such a monastery," only those monks who completed the rains-retreat in that monastery receive it until the time the Kathina is removed. If one says this from the first day of the summer, all monks present in that monastery receive it; others do not.

"Giving by designation" (ādissa deti) means giving by referring to and specifying. How? If one invites monks for gruel (yāgu) for today or tomorrow, and after they have drunk the gruel at the house, says, "I give these robes to those monks who have drunk my gruel," only those invited monks who drank the gruel receive them. The same method applies when inviting them for a meal, snacks, and so on.

"Giving to an individual" (puggalassa deti) means giving either in their absence, saying "I give this robe to the monk named so-and-so," or in their presence, placing it at their feet and saying "This robe is for you." This is the summary here; the detailed explanation has been stated in the Samantapāsādikā. Thus, by means of these eight matrix terms (mātikāpada), referring to a robe obtained by the characteristic of an out-of-season robe, it is said, "Should an out-of-season robe arise" (akālacīvaraṃ uppajjeyya).

"By one who desires" (ākaṅkhamānena) means by one who wishes. "It should be made quickly" (khippameva kāretabbaṃ) means it should be made quickly within ten days. "And if it is not sufficient" (no cassa pāripūrī) means if there is no sufficiency; the meaning is that if the cloth for making a robe sufficient for determination (adhiṭṭhāna) is not that much, but is deficient. "When there is an expectation" (satiyā paccāsāyā) means having the expectation that "On such-and-such a day the Saṅgha will receive robes, and from that, a robe for me (will be obtained)."
163:
"A robe will arise"—in this way, when there is an expectation of a robe from the Saṅgha, a group, relatives, or friends, or from any other place, such as "I will get a rag-robe" (paṃsukūla) or "I will obtain a robe with this allowable article" (kappiyabhaṇḍa), one may keep it. If one keeps it beyond that one month, it means an offence of forfeiture (nissaggiya) is incurred. If the original robe-material is fine but the expected robe-material is coarse, and they cannot be joined, or if the month is not yet full and days remain, one should not be forced to make the robe against one's will, but should make it within the period only after obtaining another expected robe-material. If one does not obtain it, the expected robe-material should also be determined as an accessory cloth (parikkhāracola).

If the original robe-material is coarse and the expected robe-material is fine, one should determine the original robe-material as an accessory cloth and keep the expected robe-material as the original robe-material. That robe again receives the one-month protection. By this method, as long as one does not obtain a suitable robe, one is allowed to keep other robes as the original robe-material. The procedure for forfeiture of this out-of-season robe should be understood by this method: "Venerable sir, this out-of-season robe of mine, having exceeded the month, is to be forfeited."

## It was laid down in the case of many monks in Sāvatthī who, having accepted out-of-season robes, let the month exceed.

It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti), and it is without command (anāṇattika). Everything hereafter is just as stated in the first Kathina training rule. The only difference is that in that training rule, it is an exceeding of ten days, whereas here it is an exceeding of one month. The rest is just the same.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Out-of-Season Robes is finished.

## 4. Purāṇacīvara Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the fourth training rule, "from one who is not a relative" (aññātikāya) means from one who is not a relative, not related by the mother's side or the father's side up to the seventh generation in any way. "By a nun" (bhikkhuniyā) means one who has been ordained in the Bhikkhu Saṅgha on one side or in the dual Saṅgha, like the Sakyan ladies. "An old robe" (purāṇacīvara) means an inner robe, an upper robe, or an outer robe that has been dyed, marked with a proper mark (kappabindu), and worn or draped at least once. At the very least, if one has traveled with it placed on the shoulder or on the head for the sake of use, or if one has slept using it as a pillow, that is also an old robe (purāṇacīvara). "Or should have it washed" (dhovāpeyya vā) means if one speaks with the words "Wash it," or makes a bodily gesture, or gives it from hand to hand, or places it at the feet, or stands within twelve cubits and throws it over, or to another's...
164:
Or if it is sent into the hands [of another], it is still considered washed or caused to be washed by that bhikkhunī. The same method applies to dyeing and causing to be beaten. If it is given for washing into the hands of a trainee (sikkhamānā), a female novice (sāmaṇerī), or a female lay follower (upāsikā), and that person washes it after having received higher ordination, it is an offense of forfeiture and confession (nissaggiya pācittiya). If it is given into the hands of a male lay follower (upāsaka) or a male novice (sāmaṇera), and that person, having changed gender and received higher ordination [as a nun], washes it; or if it is given into the hands of a young monk, and he, having changed gender, washes it [as a nun], it is also an offense of forfeiture and confession. The same method applies to dyeing and causing to be beaten. The procedure for forfeiture should be understood by this method: "Venerable sir, this old robe of mine was caused to be washed by a non-relative bhikkhunī; it is to be forfeited."

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the case of Venerable Udāyi causing an old robe to be washed. It is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇa-paññatti) [not shared with nuns]. It is an offense arising from a command (sāṇattika) because of the command "Wash [it]," etc. For a monk who so commands, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for all preliminary efforts of the bhikkhunī, such as preparing the hearth. It becomes a forfeiture (nissaggiya) as soon as it is lifted after washing, or just dyed, or just beaten. For one who causes all three acts—washing, etc.—or two acts to be done, there is one forfeiture due to the object, and wrongdoing for the others. If, however, she does all of them because he said "Wash [it]," the offense is due to the washing alone. For one who says, "Do what needs to be done to this robe," there are two wrongdoings along with one pācittiya for that single statement. There is an offense of wrongdoing for one who causes a bhikkhunī ordained only on one side (by the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha) to wash it, for one who uses it without forfeiting it, for one who causes another's property or a sitting cloth or a spread to be washed, and for one who perceives a relative as a non-relative or is in doubt. For one who perceives a non-relative as a relative or is in doubt, it is still an offense of forfeiture and confession. Hereafter, in such cases, we shall say "triad of pācittiya" (tika-pācittiya). There is no offense if a non-relative bhikkhunī who is a companion of a relative bhikkhunī washes it (without being commanded), or if she washes it without being commanded, or if she washes another requisite that has not yet been used, or if trainees and female novices wash it. There is no offense for insane persons, etc. The three factors here are: being an old robe, commanding a non-relative bhikkhunī while standing within the precinct (upacāra), and her washing it, etc. It has the origin of sañcaritta, is an act of commission (kiriya), is not excused by perception (no-saññā-vimokkha), is without criminal intent (acittaka), is a breach of regulation (paṇṇatti-vajja), is a bodily and vocal action, and involves three states of mind and three feelings.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Old Robes is finished.
165:
## 5. Cīvarappaṭiggahaṇa Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the fifth training rule, the term 'aññātikāya' (by a non-relative) is the same as the method already stated; therefore, we shall not analyze it further in any subsequent training rule. 'Cīvara' (robe) refers to any one of the six kinds of robes, such as linen or silk, that is suitable for formal assignment (vikappana); this method should be observed in all training rules related to robes. Where there is a specific difference, we shall mention it there. Regarding the word 'paṭiggaṇheyya' (should receive): whether the bhikkhunī gives it by hand into [the monk's] hand, or places it at his feet, or while he is giving a Dhamma talk and clothes are being thrown [as offerings], she throws it over him even from outside the twelve-cubit precinct—if the monk accepts it, it is considered received. However, it is allowable to receive a robe sent into the hands of any unordained person. It is also allowable to take a robe placed by a bhikkhunī on a rubbish heap, etc., with the intention 'I will take it as a refuse-rag (paṃsukūla),' by resolving upon it as a refuse-rag robe.

'Aññatra pārivattakā' (except in exchange) means: except for a robe taken in exchange by giving at least a piece of gallnut or with the intention 'I will give something [in return],' a monk who receives even a small cloth water-strainer suitable for formal assignment incurs an offense of forfeiture and confession. The procedure for forfeiture should be understood by this method: "Venerable sirs, this robe of mine was received from the hand of a non-relative bhikkhunī, other than in exchange; it is to be forfeited."

This training rule was laid down in Rājagaha concerning the case of Venerable Udāyi receiving a robe. 'Aññatra pārivattakā' is a supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) in this rule. This is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇa-paññatti) and does not involve a command (anāṇattika). There is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for efforts such as stretching out the hand to receive it. It becomes a forfeiture (nissaggiya) upon acquisition and must be forfeited. It is a triad of pācittiya. There is an offense of wrongdoing for a monk who receives from a bhikkhunī ordained only on one side, or who receives with the perception of a relative as a non-relative, or who is in doubt. There is no offense in taking by trust, temporary loan, receiving requisites that do not require formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) such as bowl-bags, receiving from the hands of trainees and female novices, or receiving from insane persons, etc. The three factors here are: being a robe suitable for formal assignment, not being an exchanged robe, and receiving from the hand of a non-relative bhikkhunī. It has the origin of sañcaritta and is an act of commission or omission (kiriyākiriya). The rest is the same as the fourth training rule.

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Receiving Robes is finished.

## 6. Aññātakaviññatti Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the sixth training rule, 'gahapati' (householder) refers to a man who is not ordained among the monks. 'Gahapatānī' (housewife) refers to a woman who is not ordained among the nuns. This method should be observed in all training rules related to householders.
166: "Viññāpeyya" means to ask for oneself or to have another ask. "Aññatra samayā" means except on the occasion when one's robe has been stolen or destroyed/lost; for the effort of asking on other occasions, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa), and upon receiving, it is an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya). In forfeiting it, the procedure of the Vinaya should be known in this way: "Venerable sir, this robe, which was asked for from an unrelated householder at a time other than the proper occasion, is to be forfeited." It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning Venerable Upananda in the matter of asking for robes. "Aññatra samayā" is a supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) in this training rule. This training rule is a common regulation (sādhāraṇapaññatti) and is not involving a command (anāṇattika). It is a pācittiya involving a triad (tikapācittiya). There is an offense of wrongdoing for one who perceives a relative as unrelated or is in doubt. There is no offense for one who asks on the proper occasion, or from a relative or one who has given an invitation, or for one who asks from another's relative or invitee on their behalf, or for one who purchases with one's own property, or for insane persons, etc. In this training rule, there are four factors: being a robe suitable for formal assignment (vikappanupaga), not being the proper occasion, asking from an unrelated person, and receiving it thereby. The origin and so forth are the same as the fourth training rule. ## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Asking from an Unrelated Person is Finished. ## 7. The Explanation of the Training Rule on More Than That In the seventh training rule, "tañce" refers to that stolen or destroyed robe. "Abhihaṭṭhuṃ" is the prefix "abhi" with "harituṃ" (to bring), meaning to take. "Pavāreyya" means to cause to desire, to arouse a wish, or to invite saying, "Take as much as you wish." Or, just as "daṭṭhu" in the phrase "nekkhammaṃ daṭṭhu khemato" means "having seen" (disvā), here too "abhihaṭṭhuṃ pavāreyya" means to bring near and place before [the monk], inviting him either by body or by speech, saying, "Take as much as you wish from our cloth-storehouse." "Santaruttaraparamaṃ" means a robe where the inner robe along with the upper robe is the maximum limit. It means the upper robe together with the inner robe is the highest limit. "Tato cīvaraṃ sāditabbaṃ" means that from those robes brought, only this many robes should be accepted, and not beyond that.
