The decision regarding the loss of robes is as follows: For a monk who has three determined robes, if all three are lost, he may accept (be satisfied with) two robes. Having worn one and draped one, he should seek another (the great robe) from a suitable place (such as from relatives, etc.). If two robes of a monk are lost, he should accept one robe. If he normally travels with only an inner robe and an upper robe, he may accept two robes. Such acceptance would be equal to a monk accepting one robe. If one out of three robes is lost, he should not accept any. If one out of two robes is lost, he should accept one. If he has only one robe and that one is lost, he may accept two.

For a nun, if all five robes are lost, she may accept two. If four are lost, she may accept one. If three are lost, she should not accept any. There is no need to mention the case of two or one being lost (as she certainly cannot accept any). Indeed, anyone should remain within the limit of an inner robe and an upper robe at most. If one makes an effort to request more than those two, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred. If they are obtained, a Nissaggiya offense is incurred. In forfeiting them, the procedure for forfeiture should be understood in this way: "Venerable sir, this robe of mine, requested from an unrelated householder beyond those two, is to be forfeited (nissaggiya)."

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks who requested many robes. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti). It is ananaṭṭika (not involving an order). It is a Pācittiya of the triple type (tika-pācittiya). If one requests from a relative thinking they are unrelated, or if one is in doubt, a Dukkaṭa offense is incurred. There is no offense for: a monk who, having made two robes, says "I will bring the remainder" and takes it; a monk who is told "Let the remainder be yours alone"; a monk who takes a robe given not because of being robbed or lost; a monk who requests from a relative or one who has given an invitation according to the stated method; a monk who purchases with his own property; or for those who are insane, etc. The four factors here are: being beyond those two robes, the absence of reasons such as being robbed, requesting from an unrelated person, and the acquisition through that request. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so on are the same as the fourth training rule.

## The Commentary on the Tatuttari Training Rule is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Upakkhaṭa Training Rule

In the eighth training rule, "specifically for a monk" means designating him, saying "I will give to such-and-named monk." "Robe-fund" (cīvaracetāpanna) refers to the price of a robe, such as gold and so on. "Should be prepared" (upakkhaṭa) means it is ready, collected and set aside. "Having exchanged" (cetāpetvā) means having exchanged, or having had it made, or having bought it. "I will clothe with a robe" is just a common way of speaking. In reality, the meaning here is "I will give to such-and-named monk."
168:
In this context, the meaning is as follows: 'Tatra ce so' refers to the place where that householder or that housewife is; if that monk, without being previously invited, approaches the place where that donor is and enters into a specification (arrangement) regarding a robe—this is the connection of the words in the phrase 'Tatra ce so'. 'Vikappaṃ āpajjeyya' means he would enter into a special arrangement or an additional provision. To show the manner in which he enters into such an arrangement, the words beginning with 'Sādhu vata' were spoken. In that phrase 'Sādhu vata', the word 'Sādhu' is an indeclinable in the sense of requesting. The word 'Vata' is an indeclinable in the sense of reflection. By the word 'maṃ', he refers to himself. By the word 'āyasmā', he addresses another. 'Evarūpaṃ vā evarūpaṃ vā' refers to one of the qualities such as length and so on. 'Kalyāṇakamyataṃ upādāya' means having taken with a mind desiring a beautiful or excellent robe; this phrase is connected with 'āpajjeyya ce'. If, due to the words of that monk who has entered into such an arrangement, the donor increases the price from what was originally intended and has a better robe exchanged (or purchased), there is an offense of Dukkaṭa for the monk's effort, and it becomes Nissaggiya (to be forfeited) upon acquisition. In that case, the procedure for forfeiture should be understood in this manner: 'Venerable sirs, this robe of mine, having approached a non-related householder who had not previously invited me and having entered into a specification, is to be forfeited.'

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning Venerable Upananda in the case of entering into a specification regarding a robe. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti). It is ananaṭṭika (not by command) because it is done by oneself. It is a Tika-pācittiya. There is an offense of Dukkaṭa for one who is in doubt or who perceives a relative as a non-relative. There is no offense for one who tells a donor desiring to purchase an expensive robe, 'Please donate a less expensive robe'; or for one who says, 'Please give another robe of this kind' with the same original price; or for one who requests from relatives or those who have invited him in the manner described; or for one who purchases with his own wealth; or for those who are insane, etc. There are three factors here: the desire for a better robe, requesting from a non-relative, and acquisition through that request. The originations (samuṭṭhāna) and so on are the same as the fourth rule.

## The Explanation of the Upakkhaṭa Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 9. Explanation of the Second Upakkhaṭa Sikkhāpada

In this ninth rule, the meaning should be understood in this very same way. This rule is similar to the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) of the previous eighth rule. The only difference here is that in the eighth rule, only one donor was made to suffer (distressed), whereas in this rule, two donors are made to suffer; this is the distinction here, everything else is exactly the same as the previous rule. Just as there is an offense for one who takes by distressing two donors, so also should the offense be understood for one who takes by distressing many donors. In the procedure for forfeiture: 'This [robe] of mine...'
169:
'Venerable sirs, this robe, having approached non-related householders who had not previously invited me and having entered into a specification, is to be forfeited.' The variation in the wording should be understood in this manner.

## The Explanation of the Second Upakkhaṭa Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 10. Explanation of the Rāja Sikkhāpada

In the tenth rule, the Rāja Sikkhāpada, 'Rājabhogga' means one who has wealth (possessions) to be enjoyed that is received from the king. There is also a reading 'Rājabhoga', which means one who has wealth or a position received from the king. 'Cīvaracetāpanna' refers to unallowable objects such as gold and so on (the robe fund). 'Pahiṇeyya' means he should send. The words beginning with 'Iminā' were spoken to show the purity of the arrival (āgamanasuddhi). Indeed, if one were to send saying, 'Give this robe fund to the monk named so-and-so,' because the source of the arrival is not pure, the monk should not even point out a steward (kappiyakāraka) regarding that robe fund which is an unallowable object.

'Ābata' means it has been brought. The words beginning with 'Na kho mayaṃ' were spoken to show that even if the robe fund is brought in an allowable way, it becomes unallowable due to such words of the messenger; therefore, it should be rejected. Indeed, gold, silver, coins (kahāpaṇa), and māsa—these four are objects of forfeiture (nissaggiya-vatthu). Pearls, gems, lapis lazuli, shells, crystal, coral, rubies, variegated stones, the seven kinds of grain, as well as female slaves, male slaves, fields, lands, flower gardens, fruit orchards, and so on—these objects of Dukkaṭa are not allowable to be accepted for oneself, or for a shrine (cetiya), the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual. Therefore, the words beginning with 'Na kho mayaṃ' were spoken to show that it is not allowable to consent to that robe fund.

However, the words 'Cīvarဉ္စ ခေါ မယံ ပဋိဂ္ဂဏှာမ' (But we do accept robes) may be spoken because the robe is brought specifically for oneself; therefore, it was said. 'Kālena' means at a proper and suitable time; the meaning is that we accept an allowable robe when we have a need for it. 'Veyyāvaccakara' means a steward (kappiyakāraka). This pointing out, 'Niddisitabbō', is permitted because the messenger asks with allowable words, 'Does the venerable one have any steward?' If, however, the messenger says, 'Who takes this?' or 'To whom shall I give it?', one should not point out a steward. The words 'An attendant (ārāmika) or a lay follower (upāsaka)' were spoken because they are suitable; however, excluding the five fellow-dhamma practitioners, any person who acts as a steward is allowable. The words 'This is he, friend' were spoken to show the monk's allowable speech; it should be spoken in this very way.
170:
In truth, one should not say, "Give it to him," and so forth. (One should only say this:) "I have instructed him" means "I have instructed him; when you have need of a robe, he will give you a robe." This is the meaning. Indeed, only when the messenger has informed [the monk] in this way is it proper to prompt for that robe; it is not proper to prompt merely because [the messenger] went after placing [the robe fund] in his hand. If, however, [the steward] is pointed out in person, saying, "This is the steward," and the messenger, in person, gives the robe fund into his hand and departs saying, "Buy a robe and give it to the Elder," then it is proper to prompt even if [the monk] does not say, "I have instructed him." If the messenger, while about to depart, says to the monk, "I will give it into his hand; you should receive the robe," or sends another to inform him, then it is also proper to prompt the other (the steward pointed out in absence). The phrase "by a messenger" is merely an illustration of the teaching. Even if a donor brings [the robe fund] himself and acts in this way, this same procedure is the mark [to be followed]. "Friend, I have need of a robe"—this is an illustration of the mark of prompting. If one prompts by speech, one should say either these words or the meaning of these words in any language; however, it is not proper to speak in such a way as "Give to me, bring for me," and so forth. "He should produce" means that by prompting three times with such speech, he should achieve it through acquisition. "In that case, it is good" means that such achievement is good.

"At most six times" is an adverbial usage (neuter singular). Indeed, the monk, intending to get the robe, should stand silently for at most six times; he should not sit, he should not receive material gifts, and he should not preach the Dhamma. If asked, "For what reason have you come?" he should only say, "Understand, friend." If he sits and so forth, he breaks the standing; he destroys the reason for coming. This is said for the purpose of showing the mark of prompting by body. Here, since three promptings and six standings are allowed as the maximum limit, twice as many standings as promptings are allowed. Therefore, if he only prompts and does not stand, he gets six promptings. If he only stands and does not prompt, he gets twelve standings. If he does both, for every one prompting, two standings must be reduced. Among those promptings and standings, if a monk goes repeatedly on a single day and prompts six times, or goes only once and says six times, "Friend, I have need of a robe," and likewise goes repeatedly on a single day and stands twelve times, or goes only once and stands in various places, he also breaks all promptings and all standings. What then...
171:
...need be said of one who acts thus on different days? This is the decision here. However, regarding stewards whom the donor himself went and pointed out, it is proper to prompt and urge them even a hundred times (many times). But regarding a mukhavevaṭika steward and a parammukha steward who are not pointed out by both [the monk and the donor], nothing should be said (one should not prompt). Thus, ten types of stewards are shown in this training rule.

'Beyond that' means beyond the limit of prompting and standing mentioned above. 'Forfeiture' (nissaggiya) means that for a monk who makes an effort beyond the limit, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) for every effort; upon acquisition, it becomes an offense of forfeiture (nissaggiya). Here, the procedure for forfeiture should be understood in this way: 'Venerable sirs, this robe of mine, produced by prompting more than three times and by standing more than six times, is to be forfeited.'

'From wherever the robe fund was brought' means the robe fund was brought for that monk from a king or a royal official. There is also a reading 'yatvassa', but the meaning is the same. 'There' means to the presence of (near) that king or royal official; for here the locative case expresses proximity. 'It does not serve any purpose for that monk' means that the robe fund does not accomplish even the slightest task for that monk.

'Let the venerable ones strive for their own' means let the venerable ones obtain their own property. 'Let not your own be lost' means let not your property be lost [in the hands of others]. 'This is the proper course there' means this speaking, either by oneself or by sending [a messenger], is the custom (vatta) that follows the supramundane Dhamma when the matter of the robe is not accomplished. Therefore, a monk who does not act thus commits an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) due to the breach of custom.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning Venerable Upananda, in the story where he did not wait when told, 'Venerable sir, please wait for just today.' This is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti) and is a training rule not involving a command (anāṇattika). There is a pācittiya in a triad (tika-pācittiya). For one who perceives it as more when the number of promptings and standings is less, or for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). There is no offense if it is obtained without prompting, if it is given by the owners after they themselves prompted [the steward], or for one who is insane, etc. Here, there are four factors: the steward being pointed out by the monk, the robe fund being entrusted by the messenger, making an effort beyond the limit, and acquisition through that effort. The originations and so forth are the same as the fourth training rule.

## 2. Eḷakaloma Vagga
## 1. Commentary on the Kosiya Training Rule
In the first training rule of the Eḷakaloma Vagga, the term "kosiyamissakaṃ" (mixed with silk) means mixed with even a single strand of silk thread, or at the very least, with silk thread blown by the force of the wind onto the place where the rug is being made. The term "santhataṃ" (a rug) refers to an object characterized by being made by spreading layers of silk threads on a level piece of ground and sprinkling them with rice-gruel water (starch) and the like. Regarding "kārāpeyya nissaggiyaṃ" (should cause to be made, it is to be forfeited), an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is committed through the efforts of making it oneself or causing another to make it; upon acquisition, it becomes an offense entailing forfeiture (nissaggiya).

In this context, the procedure for forfeiture should be understood by this method: "Venerable sir, this rug mixed with silk, which I caused to be made, is to be forfeited by me." Following the sequence of these words, the method of forfeiture for all subsequent rugs (santhata) should be understood. Since it can be understood from this much, the method of forfeiture will not be shown hereafter.

This training rule was laid down in the city of Āḷavī, concerning the group of six monks (chabbaggiya) who caused rugs mixed with silk to be made. This is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇapaṇṇatti). It is an offense involving a command (sāṇattika) by virtue of causing it to be made for one's own use. By the fourfold method, such as starting it oneself and having another finish it, four offenses entailing expiation (pācittiya) are incurred. An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is incurred in making or causing it to be made for the sake of another, as well as in using a rug made by another after acquiring it. There is no offense in making a canopy and the like, nor for those who are insane and so forth. There are three factors for this training rule: the state of being mixed with silk, making or causing the rug to be made for one's own use, and the acquisition of it. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same as the method stated in the Dhovāpana training rule.

## The Commentary on the Kosiya Training Rule ends.

## 2. Commentary on the Suddhakaḷaka Training Rule
In the second training rule, the term "suddhakaḷakānaṃ" (of pure black wool) means made of pure black wool not mixed with other colors. This was laid down in the city of Vesālī, concerning the group of six monks who made such rugs. The remaining meanings are exactly the same as the first training rule.

## The Commentary on the Suddhakaḷaka Training Rule ends.

## 3. Commentary on the Dvebhāga Training Rule
In the third training rule, "dve bhāgā" means two parts (two portions). "Ādātabbā" means they should be taken. "Gocariyānaṃ" refers to wool of a mottled or brown color. The decision in this training rule is as follows: if one wishes to make a rug with a certain amount of wool, one should weigh that wool and take two portions of black wool, one portion of white wool, and one portion of mottled wool. If the black wool exceeds the proportion by even a single strand, an offense entailing forfeiture (nissaggiya) is incurred; if it is less, it is allowable.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group of six monks who made such rugs. This training rule pertains to both action and non-action (kiriya-akiriya). The remaining points are the same as the first training rule. Furthermore, even if these three types of rugs (Kosiya, Suddhakaḷaka, and Dvebhāga) are returned after being forfeited, they are not fit to be used.

## The Commentary on the Dvebhāga Training Rule ends.

## 4. Commentary on the Chabbassa Training Rule
In the fourth training rule, "orena ce channaṃ vassānaṃ" means within six years (on this side of six years). "Aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā" means except for the formal authorization for a rug (santhata-sammuti) given by the Saṅgha to a sick monk; excluding that, if a monk who has not received such authorization makes another new rug within six years, an offense entailing forfeiture (nissaggiya) is incurred.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many monks who caused rugs to be made every year. "Aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā" is the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti) in this rule. For a monk who has obtained that authorization, it is allowable to make a rug every year at whatever place he goes, as long as his illness is not yet cured, or if it recurs after being cured. It is also allowable for him to cause one to be made for another, or to use a rug made by another after acquiring it. The remaining points are the same as the first training rule.

## The Commentary on the Chabbassa Training Rule ends.

## 5. Commentary on the Nisīdana Training Rule
In the fifth training rule, "purāṇasanthata" (an old rug) refers to a rug that has been sat upon or lain upon at least once. "Samantā" refers to a piece cut from one side, whether circular or square. This piece should be taken to the size of one Sugata span. A monk spreading a new rug may either insert that piece in one place or unravel the wool and mix it with the new wool. By unraveling and mixing it in this way, the rug is made more durable.

If it is taken in such a way that it measures one span, it should be taken thus. The monk who spreads it may spread it in one part, or he may spread it by disentangling it and mixing it with new wool; spreading it in this way makes it firmer. "Anādā ca" means doing so without taking the old rug even though it exists. If there is no old rug, it is allowable to make one without taking it; it is also allowable to make it for another or to use it after receiving it back once made.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many monks regarding the matter of discarding rugs; the rest is the same as the third training rule.

## 6. Explanation of the Eḷakaloma Training Rule

In the sixth training rule, "addhānamaggappaṭipannassa" means while traveling on a long journey known as a distance; all this is merely to illustrate the background story; in fact, there is no fault for a monk who receives and takes it lawfully anywhere. "Tiyojanaparamaṃ" means up to a distance of three leagues from the place where it was received. "Sahatthā" means it should be carried by one's own hand. "Asante hārake" means only when there is no other carrier besides oneself. If there is one, it is allowable to have that person carry it. As for oneself, if one takes even wool placed in the ear-hole without being tied with a thread, at least for the purpose of treating an ear-ache, and exceeds three leagues by one step, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkhaṭa); if one exceeds by a second step, one incurs an offense of forfeiture and expiation (nissaggiya pācittiya).

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning a certain monk regarding the matter of carrying beyond three leagues; it is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇa-paññatti), not involving a command (anāṇattika), a triad of expiation (tika-pācittiya); for one who perceives it as more or is in doubt when the distance is less than three leagues, there is an offense of wrong-doing. There is no offense for carrying it back and forth within three leagues; for carrying it further after going with the intention of staying; for carrying it after receiving back wool that was snatched or discarded; for causing another to carry it; for carrying finished goods (katabhaṇḍa) tied with at least a thread; and for those who are insane, etc. The five factors here are: the wool being unfinished goods, the first acquisition, exceeding three leagues by taking it oneself or placing it in a vehicle without another's knowledge, not being a case of carrying back and forth, and not having the intention to stay.

This training rule has the origin of wool (eḷakaloma-samuṭṭhāna), it is an action (kiriya), not a release by perception (no-saññā-vimokkha), it is without thought (acittaka), a breach of regulation (paṇṇatti-vajja), a bodily action (kāyakamma), and involves three types of consciousness and three types of feelings.

## The Explanation of the Eḷakaloma Training Rule is finished.

## 8. Explanation of the Jātarūpa Training Rule

In the eighth training rule, "jātarūparajata" means gold and silver. Furthermore, all types of currency used in trade, such as kahāpaṇa, bronze coins, wooden coins, and lac coins, are also called "rajata" in this training rule. "Uggaṇheyya vā" means taking by oneself upon seeing gold or silver given for oneself or lying in some place without an owner. "Uggaṇhāpeyya vā" means causing another to take that same gold or silver. "Upanikkhittaṃ vā sādiyeyya" means if a monk does not reject by body or speech but accepts with the mind the gold or silver offered with the words "May this be for the venerable one," whether in his presence or in his absence with the words "My gold and silver are in such and such a place, may they be for the venerable one," or offered merely by speech or by hand gestures; such a monk is said to "consent" (sādiyeyya).

However, if he desires to receive it by consenting with the mind but rejects it by body or speech saying "This is not allowable," or if he does not reject it by body or speech but, having a pure mind, does not consent saying "This is not allowable for us," then it is allowable. "Nissaggiya" means for a monk who does any of these acts like taking, etc., there is an offense of forfeiture and expiation (nissaggiya pācittiya) according to the number of items in the case of items not bound together. The monk forfeiting it should forfeit it only in the midst of the Saṅgha thus: "Venerable sirs, I have received silver; this is a matter for forfeiture for me; I forfeit this to the Saṅgha." If a layman is there...

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning the group-of-six monks in the matter of trading with money. It is a common regulation and is without an order (anāṇattika). There are two factors here: the item exchanged or the means of exchange being gold or silver, and the act of exchanging with one's own property. It is an act of commission (kiriya); the rest is as explained in the preceding training rule.

## 10. Kayavikkaya Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the tenth training rule, "of various kinds" (nānappakāraka) means many types in terms of allowable goods such as robes, etc. "Buying and selling" (kayavikkaya) means both buying and selling. A monk who takes another's allowable goods in this manner: "Give this for this," "Bring this," "Exchange this," or "Purchase this," enters into buying (kaya). A monk who gives his own allowable goods enters into selling (vikkaya). Therefore, excluding the five classes of fellow-dhamma-practitioners (sahadhammikas), if one gives one's own allowable goods and takes even the allowable goods belonging to one's mother, it is a nissaggiya offense. According to the stated characteristics, it must be forfeited to the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual. If one says, "Having eaten or taken this, bring such and such property or perform this task," and causes dye-extract etc. to be brought, or causes requisites like a water-filter to be made, or causes new work like clearing the ground to be done, the existing object must be forfeited. If the object does not exist, one should simply confess the pācittiya offense.

It was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning Venerable Upananda in the matter of buying and selling. There is no offense for a monk who asks the price, "How much is this worth?"; or for one who, wishing to take goods from an owner, sets that owner aside and appoints another (at minimum, even the owner's son or brother) as an allowable worker (kappiyakāraka) and says, "Take such and such a thing with this and give it [to me]"; or for one who says, "We have this, and we have need of such and such," and takes what is obtained with his own property; or for one who engages in buying and selling with fellow-dhamma-practitioners; or for those who are insane, etc. There are three factors here: the goods exchanged and the means of exchange being allowable objects, the other party not being a fellow-dhamma-practitioner, and entering into buying and selling. The rest is as explained in the Rūpiyasaṃvohāra Sikkhāpada.

## The Explanation of the Kayavikkaya Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 2. Ūnapañcabandhana Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the second training rule, a bowl with fewer than five mends is called 'ūnapañcabandhana'. It means the five mends are not complete. In the phrase 'with that ūnapañcabandhana bowl' (regarding requesting), the instrumental case (karaṇa-vibhatti) is used to mark the monk who has reached a certain distinction. In that text, since a bowl with no mends at all also does not complete five mends, it is stated in the word-analysis (padabhājanī): 'A bowl called ūnapañcabandhana is one with no mends or one with only one mend,' and so on. Because it is stated as 'with an ūnapañcabandhana bowl,' if a monk's bowl has five mends or has five places suitable for mending, that bowl is no longer a valid bowl (for determination). Therefore, it is allowable to request another bowl.

If there is a crack in a bowl at a place two finger-breadths below the rim, one should bore it with a bowl-drill at the lower end of that crack, fire it, and then bind it with thread, hemp rope, or lead wire. That mended place should be covered with a lead plate or some kind of resin to prevent food (āmisa) from sticking to it. That bowl should then be determined and used. Even a small hole should be bored and mended. It is also allowable to boil molasses and mix it with stone powder to repair it.

If a bowl has two cracks, or one crack four finger-breadths long, two mends should be given. If a bowl has three cracks, or one crack six finger-breadths long, three mends should be given. If a bowl has four cracks, or one crack eight finger-breadths long, four mends should be given. If a bowl has five cracks, or one crack ten finger-breadths long, that bowl—whether mended or not—is no longer a valid bowl. Another bowl should be requested. This is the decision regarding clay bowls (mattikāpatta).
180:
In the case of an iron bowl, even if there are five holes or more than five holes, if those holes are bound and smoothed with iron powder, a pin, or a circular metal plate, that very bowl should be used; another bowl should not be requested. However, if even a single hole is large and, despite being bound with a circular metal plate, it is not smooth and food or other material sticks to the bowl, then this bowl is unallowable; another bowl should be requested.

Whichever monk requests another bowl when he has an iron bowl of the type mentioned above, or a clay bowl with fewer than five mends (less than five bindings), he commits an offense of dukkaṭa for the effort; upon receiving it, he incurs an offense of Nissaggiya Pācittiya and it must be forfeited. When forfeiting, it must be forfeited in the midst of the Saṅgha; therefore, it was said, "It should be forfeited in the assembly of bhikkhus." The meaning of "in that assembly of bhikkhus" is that those monks should assemble, each bringing the bowl they have personally determined (adhiṭṭhita). Then, a monk appointed as the bowl-distributor (pattaggāhāpaka), having spoken of the existing qualities of the bowl, should address the Elder, saying, "Venerable sir, please accept this bowl." If the Elder does not like that bowl, or if he does not accept it due to being of few desires, it is allowable. However, it is an offense of dukkaṭa for an Elder who does not accept it out of compassion for the monk who requested the bowl.

If the Elder accepts it, the Elder's bowl should be given to the second Elder, and in this manner, it should be passed down to the most junior monk of the Saṅgha. The bowl relinquished by that most junior monk is called the final bowl (pattapariyanta); that bowl should be given to the monk who requested the bowl. That monk must use that bowl carefully, just like a bowl obtained through a request. If, out of loathing for that bowl, he places it in an improper place, or uses it in an unsuitable manner, or discards it, he incurs an offense of dukkaṭa.

This training rule was laid down concerning the group of six monks (chabbaggiya) in the Sakyan country regarding the matter of requesting many bowls. This is a common regulation (sādhāraṇapaññatti) and is not involving a command (anāṇattika). By requesting a bowl without binding, with one, two, three, or four bindings, or requesting a place for no binding, or a place for one, two, three, or four bindings, there are ten varieties for each bowl. In terms of requesting, there are one hundred Nissaggiya Pācittiya offenses. There is no offense for a monk whose bowl is lost, whose bowl is broken, who requests from his own relatives or those who have invited him, who requests for another from that person's relatives or those who have invited him, who obtains it with his own property, or for one who is insane, etc. These are the four factors here: the bowl being fit for determination but having fewer than five mends, it being for one's own sake, making a request without invitation, and obtaining it through that request. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same as those stated in the Cīvaradhovāpana Sikkhāpada.

## The Commentary on the Ūnapañcabandhana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Bhesajja Sikkhāpada

In the commentary on the third Bhesajja Sikkhāpada, "paṭisāyanīyāni" means those things to be tasted or consumed. By this, it is shown that there is no offense even if medicines that one has taken and stored oneself without being formally offered exceed seven days, because those medicines are not fit to be tasted or consumed. "Bhesajjāni" refers to those things that have acquired the name 'medicine,' whether they perform a medicinal function or not. "Sappi" (ghee) refers to the clarified butter of animals such as cows whose meat is allowable. "Navanīta" (fresh butter) is the same. "Tela" (oil) refers to oil produced from sesame, mustard, honey-tree (madhuka), castor (eraṇḍaka), fat (vasā), and so forth. "Madhu" (honey) refers only to the honey made by bees. "Phāṇita" (molasses/syrup) should be understood as all sugarcane products, whether uncooked or cooked without solids, derived from sugarcane juice.

"Having accepted those medicines" (tāni paṭiggahetvā) means accepting those medicines themselves, not their raw materials (such as milk, etc.). By this, it is shown that, except for oil from fat (vasātela), there is no offense for one who exceeds seven days with ghee and so forth made after accepting the raw materials of medicines derived from temporary (yāvakālika) substances. As for oil from fat, if it is accepted in the morning, cooked in the morning, and strained in the morning, it is permitted to be consumed as oil. Therefore, except for human fat, any other fat accepted in the morning and cooked by oneself, the resulting oil is allowable to be consumed for seven days without being mixed with food (āmisa). However, oil cooked and given by an unordained person (a layperson or novice) is allowable to be consumed with food on that very day in the morning. It is not allowable to cook the raw materials of other medicines derived from temporary substances oneself.

It is allowable to cook ghee or fresh butter that has already been produced oneself; however, it is not allowable to consume that ghee mixed with food even on that very day in the morning. Ghee and so forth made by an unordained person cooking milk and so forth accepted in the morning are allowable even with food on that very day in the morning. From the afternoon onwards, they are not to be swallowed; there is no offense even if seven days are exceeded.

"They are to be consumed as a hoard" (sannidhikārakaṃ paṭibhuñjitabbāni) means that medicines accepted in the morning and stored away are allowable even by consumption with food on that very day in the morning. From the afternoon onwards, those medicines, as well as those accepted in the afternoon, are to be consumed for seven days without being mixed with food. Because of the word "paṭibhuñjitabbāni" (to be consumed), there is no offense in the case of medicines determined and kept for the purpose of anointing the feet and so forth within seven days. Mustard, honey-tree, and castor seeds, which are life-long (yāvajīvika) substances, if accepted for the purpose of making oil, the oil made on that very day is a seven-day medicine (sattāhakālika). Oil made on the second day is allowable for six days; oil made on the third day for five days; and oil made on the fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh days is allowable only on that very day. If, until dawn...
182:
If it remains until dawn, it becomes a forfeiture (nissaggiya). Oil made on the eighth day should not be swallowed (consumed). However, since it is not a forfeiture-object, it is permissible for external use (application) on the body. Even if oil is not made, mustard seeds and the like received for the purpose of making oil, as well as butter and the like not directly mentioned in the Pali text, result in an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) if seven days are exceeded. Madhuka flower syrup made with cold water follows the nature of syrup. Mango syrup and the like are only temporary (yāvakālika).

Among these medicines, those that are permissible for only seven days, even if regained after being forfeited according to the Vinaya custom, are not permissible for applying to wounds or for swallowing. They should only be used for lighting lamps or for applying black color. For the physical use (application) on the body of another monk, it is permissible. If it is abandoned without attachment and then regained, it is also permissible to swallow and consume. In the case of butter and the like kept separately, or items in a single vessel that are not mixed, offenses are incurred according to the number of items.

In Sāvatthī, this was laid down regarding many monks concerning the matter of exceeding seven days. The rest should be understood in the same manner as stated in the first training rule of the Robe Chapter (Cīvara-vagga).

## The Explanation of the Training Rule on Medicine is finished.

## 4. The Explanation of the Training Rule on the Rainy-Season Robe

In the fourth training rule, "one month remains of the four months of summer" means the last month of the four summer months remains. "Should be sought" means from the first day of the last month of summer until the last day of the month of Kattika, it should be sought by reminding, such as "it is the time for the rainy-season robe," or from a place where the Saṅgha has been invited, or by requesting from one's own relatives or those who have invited, saying "please give me a rainy-season robe." If one reminds (satupādakaraṇa) those who are not relatives or have not invited, it is a breach of conduct resulting in an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). In any case, if one requests by saying "please give me," etc., it is a forfeiture and expiation (nissaggiya pācittiya) according to the training rule on requesting from non-relatives.

"Should be made and worn" means from the first day of the last half-month of summer until the last day of the month of Kattika, it should be worn after completing the sewing, dyeing it once just to change the color, and making the proper mark (kappabindu). By this much, the last month of summer...
183:
...the last month is the period for seeking, and the last half-month is also the period for making, dyeing, marking, and wearing. This meaning is shown: that all such actions as seeking are permissible throughout the four months of the rainy season. In this month allowed as the last month of the summer, even if it is a rainy-season robe that has been sought, made, and dyed, it is not permissible to formally determine (adhiṭṭhāna) it. If the rainy season is postponed (intercalary month) after that last month has passed, one again receives a month of protection. That robe should be washed and set aside, and then formally determined on the day of entering the rains. If it has not been made due to forgetfulness or due to insufficiency of material, one receives protection for those two months and the four months of the rainy season, totaling six months. If the Kathina robe is spread in the month of Kattika, one receives another four months, thus making it ten months. Even after those ten months, for a monk who keeps that cloth as a basic robe with the hope of obtaining a robe, he receives one more month, thus receiving protection for eleven months in total. Beyond these eleven months, one does not receive protection for even a single day.

"If less than a month remains of the summer" means from the last month of summer counting back until the first day of winter. "Should seek" means for one who seeks by reminding those who are not relatives or have not invited during these seven "back-season" months, there is an offense of forfeiture and expiation (nissaggiya pācittiya). If one requests from a non-relative, there is a nissaggiya pācittiya according to the training rule on requesting from non-relatives. If one requests from a relative or one who has invited, there is no offense by that training rule, but if one reminds them, there is an offense by this training rule. "If less than a half-month remains of the summer" means within the half-month on this side of the last half-month of summer. "Having made, should wear" means for a monk who makes and wears even a robe obtained rightfully within this half-month, there is an offense of forfeiture and expiation (nissaggiya pācittiya).

In Sāvatthī, it was laid down regarding the group of six monks concerning the matter of seeking a rainy-season robe. This is an uncommon regulation (asādhāraṇa-paññatti), not involving an order (anāṇattika), and a triad of expiation (tika-pācittiya). For one who perceives it as more or is in doubt when it is less than a month or a half-month, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). Likewise, for one who lets the rain fall on his naked body when a rainy-season robe is available, there is an offense of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa). However, there is no offense for one bathing in ponds and the like, or for one whose robe has been snatched away or lost, or for one wearing it in times of danger such as "thieves will take it if not worn," or for the insane, etc.

Here, the factors for the offense of seeking are: intending for oneself, seeking at the wrong time, and obtaining it through that seeking. The factors for the offense of wearing are: having another robe, absence of danger, being one's own property, and wearing at the wrong time. The fourth training rule is finished.
184:
Having another robe to wear besides the rain-cloth, the absence of danger, the rain-cloth being one's own property, and wearing it at an improper time—these four are the factors for the offense of wearing [the rain-cloth]. The origin and so forth are the same as the method stated in the Dhovāpana Sikkhāpada.

## The Explanation of the Vassikasāṭika Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Cīvara-acchindana Sikkhāpada
In the fifth (Cīvara-acchindana) Sikkhāpada, "having given the robe oneself" (sāmaṃ cīvaraṃ datvā) means giving it oneself while expecting services and so forth. "Should snatch back" (acchindeyya) means that for a monk who, seeing that services and so forth are not performed, snatches it back with the perception that it is his own property, there are offenses according to the number of items. In the phrase "should cause to be snatched back" (acchindāpeyya), there is a dukkaṭa offense for the command "Snatch it back!" When it has been snatched back, there are offenses according to the number of robes commanded.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning Venerable Upananda in the case of snatching back a robe. It is a common regulation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti). It is with command (sāṇattika). There is a triad of pācittiya (tika-pācittiya). There is a dukkaṭa offense for one who perceives a non-ordained person (anupasampanna) as ordained, or is in doubt, or perceives him as non-ordained; or for one who snatches any other requisite such as a bowl, excluding the final robe that is capable of being assigned (vikappanūpaga), from an ordained person; or for one who snatches any requisite from a non-ordained person. There is no offense for taking a robe given back by that monk whether he is pleased or angry, or taking it out of trust (vissāsa), or for insane persons and so forth. The five factors for this training rule are: it being the final robe capable of being assigned, having given it oneself, the perception of it being one's own property, the victim being an ordained person, and snatching it back or causing it to be snatched back out of anger. The origin and so forth are the same as for taking what is not given (adinnādāna), except for the feeling (vedanā). In this training rule, the feeling is exclusively painful feeling (dukkha-vedanā).

## The Explanation of the Cīvara-acchindana Sikkhāpada is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Suttaviññatti Sikkhāpada
In the sixth (Suttaviññatti) Sikkhāpada, "thread" (suttaṃ) means the six kinds of thread such as linen thread or those similar to them. "Having asked for" (viññāpetvā) means requesting for the sake of a robe. "Should have it woven" (vāyāpeyya) means having it woven through an improper request such as "Friends, weave a robe for me." "Nissaggiya" means...
186:
"Vikappaṃ āpajjeyya" means to arrive at a special arrangement or an exceeding arrangement. To show in what manner one arrives at such an arrangement, the words beginning with "Idaṃ kho āvuso" are spoken. In that context, "āyata" means long in length. "Vitthata" means wide in breadth. "Appita" means thick and dense. "Suvīta" means well-woven, having been woven evenly in all places. "Suppavāyita" means well-stretched, having been spread evenly on the loom in all places. "Suvilekhita" means well-scraped with a scraping tool (lekhanī). "Suvitacchita" means well-brushed with a comb (koccha), meaning it has been well-washed and cleaned without leaving any residue.

Regarding "piṇḍapātamattampi," the robe does not become nissaggiya merely by the monk giving a meal. However, if those weavers, due to the monk's words, take extra thread from the hands of the robe-owners and make it even slightly longer, wider, or thicker, then during that effort (payoga), a dukkaṭa offense is incurred by the monk; upon receiving it, a nissaggiya pācittiya offense is incurred.

This training rule was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning Venerable Upananda in the case of making an arrangement (vikappa) for a robe. It is a general regulation (sādhāraṇapaññatti). It is not by command (anāṇattika). It is a tika-pācittiya. If one perceives a relative as a non-relative, or is in doubt, a dukkaṭa offense is incurred. There is no offense for having robes woven by the weavers of relatives or those who have given an invitation, for weaving for another person, for weaving with one's own wealth, for making a donor who wishes to have an expensive robe woven have a less expensive one woven instead, or for those who are insane, etc. The four factors here are: (1) approaching weavers who are not relatives and have not given an invitation to make an arrangement, (2) the robe being intended for oneself, (3) the increase of thread due to one's words, and (4) the acquisition of the robe. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth are the same as the method stated in the Dhovanapāsikkhāpada.

## The Explanation of the Mahāpesakāra Sikkhāpada is Finished.

## 8. Accekacīvara Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the eighth training rule, "dasāhānāgataṃ" means ten days have not yet arrived (ten days remaining). The word "dasāhānāgataṃ" uses the accusative case in the sense of the locative (time) by virtue of continuous connection (accantasaṃyoga). "Kattikatemāsikapuṇṇamaṃ" refers to the first Kattika full moon day (the full moon of Thadingyut). Here too, the accusative case is used in the sense of the locative, consistent with the preceding term. The meaning is this: from ten days before the first Pavāraṇā day, it is called "dasāhānāgata." If an urgent robe (accekacīvara) should arise continuously for a monk during those days, the monk, knowing "this is an urgent robe"...
187:
...the monk may accept all of it. By that passage, the storage period (the time it may be kept without formal determination or assignment) for a robe arising from the fifth day of the waxing moon of the Pavāraṇā month is shown. Although this robe storage period could indeed be established by the passage "dasāhaparamantirekacīvaraṃ dhāretabbaṃ" (an extra robe may be kept for at most ten days), the training rule was laid down by showing the meaning as if it were new, by virtue of the specific occasion that arose.

An "accekacīvara" (urgent robe) is a robe given by any person among those who are about to go on a journey, the sick, the pregnant, or those with newly arisen faith, after having announced, "I will give a rains-residence robe (vassāvāsika)." If that robe is distributed before the Pavāraṇā day, the monk who receives it should not break his rains-residence; if he does break the rains-residence, that robe becomes the property of the Saṅgha. "Until the robe-season time" means that if the Kathina has not been spread, it may be kept until the month of Tazaungmon, which is the last month of the rainy season; if the Kathina has been spread, it may be kept for five months.

This was laid down in Sāvatthī concerning many monks in the case of exceeding the robe-season time for an urgent robe. The rest of the procedure here should be understood in the same way as the method stated in the first training rule of the Cīvara Vagga.

The Explanation of the Accekacīvara Sikkhāpada is Finished.

## 9. Sāsaṅka Sikkhāpada Vaṇṇanā

In the ninth training rule, in the passage "upavassaṃ kho pana," the meaning of the word "upavassaṃ" is "upavassa" (having stayed near/spent the rains). Just as in passages like "upasampajja," the nasal (anunāsika/niggahīta) should be understood here; it means having entered and spent the rains. This word is connected with the passage "tathārūpesu bhikkhu senāsanesu viharanto." The meaning is this: having entered and spent the rains, and after that, until the end of the period of the full moon associated with the last Kattika constellation (the full moon of Tazaungmon), whatever forest dwellings there are... [pe]... may be kept inside a house.

In that passage, "āraññakāni" (forest dwellings) refers to dwellings constructed in a place at a distance of five hundred bow-lengths, measured by the bow of a teacher with the string drawn, starting from the village threshold (indakhīla) at the very back of all dwellings. If the village is unfenced, it should be measured starting from the place where a fence ought to be (a stone's throw from the edge of the village premises). If the monastery is fenced, it is measured up to that fence; if it is an unfenced monastery, it is measured up to the first dwelling, or shrine (cetiya), or Bodhi tree, or regular meeting place encountered from the direction of the village...
188:
As long as that [area] remains, it must be measured only by the standard path. It is not proper to measure by making a new path or by an area that is not a path. "Sāsaṅkasammatāni" means those recognized as "suspect" because of seeing the dwelling places of thieves and so on; this is the meaning. Because they are accompanied by fear, they are called "sappaṭibhayāni" (dangerous). This means having strong imminent danger because of seeing people being killed, robbed, or beaten by thieves.

"Antaraghare nikkhipeyya" means one may keep [the robe] in a village where one goes for alms that one especially likes, in any of the directions surrounding the forest dwelling. However, such keeping is possible only when the factors are fulfilled. These factors are as follows: One must have entered the first rains-retreat and performed the invitation (pavāraṇā) at the Mahāpavāraṇā; this is one factor. It must be the month of Kattika; this is the second factor. The dwelling must be of the minimum required distance of five hundred bow-lengths; this is the third factor. One does not get [permission to keep the robe] in a dwelling that is less than that distance or in one that is more than one gāvuta away. Only such a dwelling from which one can return to the monastery by mealtime after wandering for alms is intended in this training rule. The dwelling must be both suspect and dangerous; this is the fourth factor. "Koci deva paccayo" means some cause or reason. "Tena cīvarena" means with that robe kept in the village. "Vippavāsāya" means for the purpose of staying apart from. "Tato ce uttari vippavaseyya" means letting the seventh dawn rise in that dwelling beyond six nights. However, a monk who is unable [to return] should enter the village boundary and stay in a rest-house or anywhere, and only after knowing the status of the robe is it proper to depart. "Aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā" means except for the formal agreement (sammuti) given by the Saṅgha to a sick monk to stay apart from his robe; for one who has not obtained the agreement and stays apart for more than six nights, there is an offense of Nissaggiya Pācittiya.

This was enacted in Sāvatthī concerning many monks regarding the matter of staying apart from robes. The rest should be understood in the same manner as stated in the second training rule of the Cīvara Vagga.

## The Explanation of the Sāsaṅka Training Rule is finished.

## 10. Explanation of the Pariṇata Training Rule

In the tenth training rule, "saṅghikaṃ" means belonging to the Saṅgha. Because it has been allocated (pariṇata) to the Saṅgha, even if it has not yet reached their hands, it belongs to the Saṅgha in a certain sense. "Lābhaṃ" means the objects such as robes that are to be received. "Pariṇataṃ" means [allocated] by breaking into speech saying, "We will give, we will make,"
189:
or by hand gestures, being inclined towards the Saṅgha. "Attano pariṇāmeyya" means making it inclined towards oneself by saying, "Give this to me," and so on. If, however, it has already been given to the Saṅgha, it is not proper to take it; it must be given only to the Saṅgha. For one who diverts what is allocated to fellow practitioners, or to laypeople, or even at the minimum, to one's mother, to oneself, there is a Dukkaṭa offense for the effort (payoga), and a Nissaggiya Pācittiya offense upon acquisition (paṭilābha).

This training rule was enacted in Sāvatthī concerning the group-of-six monks regarding the matter of diverting [offerings]. It is a common rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti) and is anāṇattika (not involving a command). There is a Dukkaṭa offense for: one who is doubtful about what is already diverted; one who perceives what is not diverted as diverted; one who is doubtful about it; and one who diverts what is allocated to any one of the Saṅgha, a shrine (cetiya), or an individual to another Saṅgha and so on. There is no offense for: one who perceives it as not diverted; one who, when asked "Where shall we give?", says "Give wherever your heart is inspired, wherever your gift may be of use," and so on; and for those who are insane, etc. The three factors here are: the state of being diverted to the Saṅgha, knowing that it is diverted and diverting it to oneself, and the acquisition. The origins (samuṭṭhāna) and so on are similar to the Adinnādāna training rule.

## The Explanation of the Pariṇata Training Rule is finished.
